summary: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 67 and 1966 67. In respect of the assessment year 1967 67, the Wealth Tax Officer determined the net wealth of the assessee at Rs. 1, 50, 000 / on the valuation date. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assets were not confined to cash but also included the value of the rights in the property which constituted the asset of the deceased. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Wealth tax officer. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the Revenue. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle underlying section 7 (1) is that the gross wealth of an assessee should be taken into account when determining his net wealth. [ 249 B ] 2. The expression " net wealth " has been defined under sub section (I) of section 2 of the Act as the aggregate value of all the assets of the person liable to pay wealth tax. The definition of " net Wealth " given in section 2 (m) of the Income Tax Act includes " net assets " of any person or association of persons whether incorporated or not. The word'net wealth'is defined in Explanation (b) to section 2. Sub clause (i) of clause (m), defines the term " net asset " as including all income derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation and declared by the Supreme Court in Commissioner of Wealth Tax vs Vy sy araju B adre en arayana Mo orthy Raju (Orissa). 3. Section 3 of the Indian Wealth Tax Act, 1957 defines " net income " as meaning inter alia, all income, profits and gains accruing or arising, directly or indirectly, through or from any business connection in India or through any other person, but does not include any receipt of income, either by way of rent, interest, commission or remuneration or any other amount payable to a person in respect of any liability incurred by him in relation to the net Wealth of the estate or business of the asses ment. 4. The question whether the assets are to be included in the net assets of an asses ee under the Wealth Act is no longer res integra. In view of the decision of this Court in Ved rev u Venk appa Rao (supra), it is clear that the provisions of section 7 of the Valuation Act would apply only to cash, its value, which is determined pursuant to sub section 1 of section 3 of that Act.

The respondent was a Government servant. He was dismissed from service by the appellant on the ground that he had not been given proper opportunity to defend himself and, therefore, his dismissal order was bad in law. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the charges against him were proved. In the departmental enquiry, the Enquiry Officer found the respondent guilty of misconduct and imposed punishment of removal from service. The Tribunal set aside the order of dismissal on the grounds that the respondent had failed to maintain devotion to duty and acted in a manner which is unbecoming of a public servant. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The findings recorded by the Inquiry Officer are based on evidence and cannot be interfered with. [ 37 A ] 2. The respondent has been charged with misconduct for having failed to do so. The charge framed against him was vague ly framed as'no such person can be said to have committed any act prejudicial to the interest of the department '. The Tribunal has rightly held that it was not a case of'no work no pay ', but a case where the delinquent employee was found to be a very serious officer. The finding of the Tribunal that the Respondent was guilty of negligence or other misconduct is un disturbed. [ 38 E F ] 3. The High Court has also held that there was no evidence to hold that the disciplinary authority had passed an order of penalty without giving any reasonable opportunity to the respondent to defend. It is true that the Tribunal did not consider the question whether the respondent was guilty or not. But the fact remains that the Disciplinary Authority had not applied its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. The conclusion reached by the Tribunal is perverse. [ 39 G H;

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he was a trespasser and had been in possession of the land since June 1968. He also alleged that the respondent No. 1, the Land lord, had illegally dispossessed him from the land in question. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff had failed to prove his case that he had been forcibly eject ed by the defendant No. 2. On appeal, the District Judge allowed the appeal and set aside the decree passed by the Trial Court. In second appeal, it was contended before this Court that the High Court erred in law in allowing the appeal against the judgment of the Trial court without framing any substantial questions of law as required under section 100 (4) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of Order 7 Rule 10 CPC are not exhaustive of all situations which may arise in regard to suits or proceedings between the same parties. They are only two classes of suits; one where the cause of action is based on the same cause of actions and the other where the relief claimed is substantially the same. [ 10 D E ] 2. 1 Section 8 (2) of Act provides that no suit shall be instituted by a person against the Central Government or any State Government or against a public officer in respect of anything done or purporting to be done in good faith under this Act or rules made thereunder except with the previous permission of the concerned authority. Under sub section (2), if such person is the Central or State Government, then the jurisdiction of the Civil Court would be barred. [ 11 C F ] 2.( i) The expression " civil court " has been defined in section 2 (d) of Civil P. C. and includes a Tribunal constituted under the Act. It is clear from the definition of the term'Court'contained in section 3 (c) of, the Code that the Civil Courts have been given exclusive jurisdiction to decide the disputes relating to immovable property. This provision does not apply to the present case because the dispute involved in the suit is about the title of the property. [ 12 B C ] (ii) The suit having been filed in the year 1969, the Civil court had jurisdiction to deal with the matter. [ 13 G H ] (iii) The plaint in the instant case was filed in July, 1969. The suit was filed on November 6, 1969 when the Civil Judge refused to grant leave to the defendants to file a written statement. The trial court rejected the application for stay of the suit on the grounds that the suit was barred by limitation. [ 14 G H;

The petitioners are working as Car p enters in the Corporation. They were employed by a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and they were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 600 per month. The petitioners claim that their services should be regularised with effect from April 1, 1987. The Government issued an order on June 11, 1986 directing the petitioners to pay minimum wages prescribed by the notification dated March 19, 1986. The petitioner's case was that since the petitioners had been performing work for more than six months continuously, they could not be treated as " equal pay " for purposes of payment of wages. The State Government rejected the claim of the petitioners on the ground that there was no regular employment between the petitioners and the Company. The writ petition filed by the petitioners before this Court was dismissed by this Court. In appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the petitioners were entitled to the minimum wages payable to them under Exhibit P. 2; (ii) that the petitioners cannot enforce the right to " equal work ", inasmuch as, the petitioners did not satisfy the requirement of the definition of " equal wages " in section 2 (b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; (iii) that even though the petitioners have been discharging similar duties, they are being paid only higher wages than what is payable to other workmen; (iv) that, the fact that the employees of the Corporation are doing identical work has no relevance to the present controversy; and (v) that if the petitioners are treated as different employers, then the principle of " Equal Pay for Equal Work " would apply. Dismis sing the petitions, HELD: (1) The petitioners do not fall within the same class of employees in the same establishment. [ 669 G ] (2) The principle of equal pay for equal work does not come into play in any other establishments like the present one. If the petitioners can be treated differently, the principle will apply. It must be held that the principle " equal wage " cannot be enforced.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the late Maharaja of Vizianagaram, was the absolute owner of certain properties. She executed two documents in favour of her son and grand sons on January 14, 1944, one for Rs. 10, 000 / and another for Rs, 500 / by way of gift. In respect of these two items she executed a will on February 16, 19 02, beque ath ing all her properties to the appellant. On August 31, 1946, she executed an agreement with the respondent's father under which she conveyed to him the property covered by the will a life interest in the properties mentioned therein. After his death, the appellant filed a suit against the respondent for possession of the said properties alleging that the said document was not genuine and that it was obtained by fraud and misrepresentation. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the suit holding that the document was a sham and nominal transaction and that the appellant had failed to prove that the execution of the will was free from suspicion. It further held that the respondent had failed in proving that the will dated August 31. 55 was a forged document and that he had no right or title to execute the will. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show that the testator had signed the will in order to create a bar against the execution thereof. [ 463 E ] (2) There is nothing in the deed to show how many tenants were living together at the time of the execution and what was the condition of the testator when he executed the will and whether the will contained any such terms as to leave any doubt about its genuineness. [ 464 B C ] (3) The fact that the exec utant did not know exactly what transpired in the execution proceedings shows that he knew nothing about the execution nor did he know anything about the contents of the Will. He did not remember if he had seen the testator signing the will before he got it written down. If he knew what was written in the will he would have stated so in the document. But, in the absence of any explanation as to why he did not mention the words " I am deposing falsely ", the High court was justified in rejecting the contention of the appellant that the attesting witnesses should be called upon to explain their conduct.

The appellants are manufacturers of electric energy apparatus and other electrical appliances. They were paying duty on the goods manufactured by them at their factory in Andhra Pradesh, but they did not pay any excise duty on such goods. The Assistant Collector held that the goods under consideration were covered by entry No. 4 of Schedule I to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 (as amended) and therefore liable to be taxed under the said entry. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that it was a " cinema ar c carbon's " which were used for cin em as and that the expression " elect ro ly tic so da " meant only those mechanical appliances which could be used for the purpose of making the product fit for use as an aid or addition. The High Court also took the view that the word " elect rode " in Entry No. 6 would cover all kinds of apparatus used in the process of manufacture of electric ally lighting power ed du ct etc., and that even if it was intended to confine the entry to certain types of apparatus, there was no reason why the expression'elect ro mag ne tic apparatus'should have been construed as meaning only the apparatus designed for the particular purpose. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended that the words " elect ri fied or equipped with electric ther m ome ter " in entry No, 4 mean that the electric ian itself is capable of being used as an ap pliance for the purposes mentioned therein. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. It is true that the term " elect rol our " has been used in various parts of the definition section. But it cannot be said that the intention of the fram ers of the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use in project ors or other cin emato graphic equipment can be inferred from the fact that some gu ides or uses are required for use. [ 7 E ] 2. The word " access ory " is defined in Section 3 (f) of the Andhra Act as follows: " Access ory means the physical object produced by a motor vehicle when used for its own use or where the motor vehicle is fitted with either a device or two or more than one electric ally operated device; and includes any part thereof, and any fittings affixed thereto for the more beneficial enjoyment of the same." The word'access ory'is defined as " the assembly of a motor vehicles, or of a system, device or apparatus, or both, for the conveyance of human being's or animals ". The word access ory is defined to mean " access ories for use, such as electric ally he ated, controlled, or power ed ". The first part of the entry deals with the supply of electrical energy. The second part relates to electrical appliances and apparatus. The third part relates only to electrical apparatus and apparatus for recording sound and radi ation. The last part of item No. 5 refers to electrical machinery and apparatus of electrical system.

The petitioners are owners of quarrying lim estone in the State of Gujarat. They had a quarry lease for quarrying lim bs and they were granted leases by the State Government under section 14 (1) of the Act to excav ate minor minerals from their lands. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said provisions on various grounds, inter alia, that the royalty was not payable as per the rules and that the mining lease was void because it did not contain any provision for regulating the grant of mining leases or for granting of mining lease. It was also contended that the provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, which required the prior approval of the Central Government before issuing the notification could be enforced only if there was a valid reference made to the State Legislature. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the petitioners had no right to challenge the validity or otherwise of the provisions contained in Chapter III of the Rules. Dismis sing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred upon the State Governments under Section 15 of the, is an enabling provision and cannot be construed as authorising the State to make a classification between'minor minerals'and'minor mineral '. [ 416 C ] 2. The contention that the State has no power to make rule prescribing the manner in which the tax can be imposed must therefore fail. [ 416 F G ] 3. The State Government has the power to issue a notification specifying the rate at which royalty shall be levied on minor minerals. This power can be exercised subject to certain conditions. The proviso to sub section (1), however, provides that such notification may provide that the rates of royalty shall not exceed the amount specified therein. The impugned notifications do not impose any obligation on the State Govern ment to levy royalty in respect of minor minerals but merely fix es the minimum amount of royalty payable by the lessees. There is nothing in the Act requiring the State government to specify the maximum limit of royalty in regard to minor minerals provided in the proviso to Rule 21. [ 418 E H; 420 A B ] 4. The object underlying the provisions is to ensure that the existing lessees who have been granted a contract with the State should pay royalty to the owner of the land within the period fixed by the rules. If the lessee fails to pay the royalty, he will be liable to prosecution under section 9 of the Indian E ase ments Act, 1882. But where the State does not prescribe any specific mode for determining the royalty payable, the State is entitled to enforce the liability to pay royalty in case of default. [ 419 D E ] 5. The fact that the petitioner had paid royalty in excess of what was prescribed would not make him liable to pay any royalty. He had to pay compensation for the loss suffered by him due to illegal extraction of minerals. [ 420 E ] 6. The Orissa Minor Mineral Rules, 1966 deal with the fixation of royalty and the procedure to be followed in imposing the same. The rules framed under the Act do not require the State Govt. to impose any royalty in the matter of granting a prospecting licence or a mining lease in respect thereof. The Rules Decision and Holding: The State of Karnataka has no authority to impose a royalty in terms of the Mining Concession's Rules, 1950.

The appellant was appointed as a trustee of the temple in 1920. He died on March 31, 1968. His widow and son were nominated by his widow for succession to the office of trustee. In 1956 he filed a suit against the trustees of the math for a declaration that the trust deed executed by him in favour of the first respondent was void and inoperative. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal preferred by the respondents holding that the trustee had no right to nominate the successor to the trustee under the law of inheritance. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the manager of a religious institution is not an " officer " within the meaning of section 6 (9) of the Act and therefore the appointment of the trustee was invalid. HELD: The expression'hereditary trustee'occurring in section 6 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1939, means a person who has got a right or interest in any property which is personal to the Mahant or to any other person. A person may be appointed as trustee only if he possesses some special custom entitling him to succeed to the estate of the deceased. It is not possible to say that there is a vacancy and B is elected to that office. [ 535 G H ] The word'succession'is defined in section 2 (9). The term'hereditary'is used in section 3 (9), which provides that every person shall have the same meaning as is assigned to it in clause (b) of section 2 of the Indian Succession Act, 18 65. Section 6 (1) defines'hereditary office '.'hereditary succession'means succession among the members of the family of the last male holder.'hereditary right'is one of the incidents of a person's duty to perform service. The hereditary right of a hereditary trustee is not merely an incident of the office but is a right to hold property. The right of the succeeding trustee is a cre ature of statute. The legislature could not have intended such a provision to be so construed as to defeat the very object of the legislature. The definition of hereditary trustee in section 6A (9)( a) of Act 19 of 1951 must be read with section 6. The word hereditary'would include even such cases. The contention that the hereditary trustee cannot survive after the expiry of one year from the date of nomination is untenable. The fact of the transmission of the rights, estate, obligations and charges of a deceased person to his heir or heirs does not result in the substitution of the hereditary right to the present incumbent. The mere fact that a member of the managing committee dies without leaving any heir will not make him a hereditary administrator. The removal of a trustee is dependent upon the consent of the f ounder. The continuance of the manager is not dependent on the volition of the new trustee. The change of the terms of the endowment is not a hereditary right. The position of a she ba it is a hereditary office. The manager ship of a math is a permanent feature. The f ounder has a share in the management of the property. He can succeed to his own office. If Decision and Holding: The question whether a man can succeed in the office to another, is a matter of discretion. There is no rule of Hindu law that a man should not succeed to himself because a retiring trustee is eligible for succession. The decision of the Privy Council in Sri Mahant Param Das Goswami vs Radhakrishna Das (I. L. R., referred to.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for causing the murder of his brother. He was sentenced to death and also to rigorous imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of death on the ground that there were only two persons who had been named in the first information report and that they were not even known to the witnesses when he went to the place of occurrence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the evidence of PW 4 is not corroborated by the contents of the FIR; (2) that the prosecution case should be believed as a whole and that the testimony of PW 3 is wholly reliable; and (3) that PW 4's version in the First Information Report is inconsistent with the contents thereof. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The High Court has rightly rejected the testimony to come to an un hes it ating conclusion that the deceased was alone or in near relation to the accused. [ 712 G ] (ii) It is well settled that if the court accepts the testimony given by the witness in the court as being wholly reliable, it may look for corroboration from other independent sources. If the court finds that the witness is absolutely reliable, its credibility cannot be doubted. But where the witness stands wholly corroborated by some independent evidence, such as the statement of the witness himself, which is not free from doubt, then the court can act upon it without seeking corroboration from any independent source. [ 713 B C ] (iii) There are several circumstances which go to show that the appellant was one among the assailants. When the appellant came running away after the assault, the deceased ran towards him and started assaulting him with knife, but the appellant inflicted injury on the neck of the deceased with a knife. The appellant gave a blow with the knife on the head of the injured. The deceased fell down and died immediately thereafter. The injuries caused to the deceased clearly point to the presence of the accused at the place where he fell down. [ 714 F H ] (iv) The conduct of the eye witnesses shows that they all saw the appellant inflicting stab wounds on the deceased. They did not see the assailants who might have escaped. Nor could they have seen the assailants actually attack ing the deceased immediately after the incident. [ 715 D E ] (v) The medical evidence does not support the version of the complainant about the participation of the assailant in the commission of the crime. [ 716 A ] (vi) The fact that the witnesses were afraid to speak falsely against the accused would not mean that they would not mention about the identity of the culpr it. [ 717 B ] (vii) The evidence of the sole eye witness is not acceptable because the witness was wholly unreliable.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself, his wife and two minor sons. In the year 1948 the appellant became its Kar ta in respect of the business carried on by him as an individual. He died leaving behind his widow and three daughters. On April 1, 1950, he made a return under section 24 B (2) of the Income tax Act, 1922 for the assessment years 1950 51 to 1951 52 and 1952 53. The income tax officer assessed the total income of the deceased at Rs. 43, 162 / 11 / 3 and Rs. 32, 523 / 64 / 4 / 44, respectively. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount received by the heirs and legal representatives of the assessee was liable to be taxed in the hands of the heirs as provided in section 24 A of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal but allowed the claim for exemption from tax. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Held: (i) The liability to pay tax arises only when there is a receipt of the income or any part thereof; it cannot be said that the income has been received in the previous year. If the income had not been received by a person who is not liable to tax in the earlier year, then the question whether the income can be deemed to have been received must arise only if the income is received in that previous year and not in the subsequent year. (ii) Where the income received in one year is liable to income tax in another year, the income may be deemed by fiction to have accrued to the person during that year. But where the income was received before the date of the previous years and is not taxable in the first year, no income can accrue to the assessee until the income comes to tax. (iii) Section 24 B does not apply to cases covered by section 24 C. (iv) The scheme of section 24 E is that where the Income Tax Officer is not satisfied with the explanation offered by the assessee, he will proceed to assess the income of such person after giving notice to the other party and also determine the amount of tax due from the estate of the person concerned. (v) Where a person fails to furnish the return within the time specified in sub section (1), the Income - tax Officer shall serve upon him a notice requiring him, on payment of the sum specified therein, to pay the amount within the period specified in the notice.

The petitioners were employed by the Andhra Pradesh State Government in the Public Works Department of the former Hyderabad State. They claimed that they had been appointed as Office Assistants and were paid their salaries from the out of the State funds, but the respondents contended that the petitioners were not entitled to any salary for the period prior to the appointment or employment of the petitioners. The High Court held that section 3 of the Act was ultra vires because it provided only for the appointment of office staff and did not provide for any age qualification. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 3 of The Public Employment (Require ment as to Res idence) Act, 1957 is a provision enacted with a view to make certain appointments under the Constitution possible without any limitation or restriction on the tenure of the office or employment. It does not speak of residence within the State or Union territory. [ 12 G H ] (2) The words'any requirement " are wide enough to include the requirement of residence in a particular part of the state. There can be no doubt that the expression'any condition'used in section 3 must be given its natural meaning. The word'residence'has been defined in section 2 (e) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 which means that where there is no specific mention of residence, the word'occupation'would mean the last place of residence mentioned in the definition. [ 13 B C ] (3) The expression'residence in any particular part'occurring in section 4 (1)( b) of The General Clauses act, 1897 cannot be read to mean that the general term'residence within a particular State'should mean the place where the office of the officer is situated. If the intention of the legislature was to leave the matter to the discretion of the executive authority, it could have expressed an intention that the Central or State Government should prescribe the requisite number of residence. But if the intention was to make a law prescribing the conditions of residence of persons who may be employed in the public service, then such a clause will not be effective unless it is expressly stated to the contrary. The appellant was convicted of the offence under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898. He was acquitted by the trial court but on appeal by the State he was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of six months and seven days. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against him. In appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the presumption under section 55 of the Act could not be made available in respect of the articles found in the al mir ah; (ii) the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles were in the exclusive possession of the appellant when they went out of the house and thus there was no evidence as to how they came into the possession of any person other than the appellant; and (iii) the courts below erred in holding that the appellant had secre ted the letters in question from the house where the dead body lay. HELD: (1) The presumption arising under section 7 of the Evidence Act is one of the degree of proof which can be applied to a civil case. It is open to the accused to establish that the letters recovered from the possession or belonged to him. [ 608 E F ] (2) The burden of proving that the letter was in the joint possession of both the accused and the complainant's father rests upon the fact whether the letters were in their exclusive possession or not. If the presumption is drawn from the fact that the two letters are in the custody of the accused then the presumption would arise that those letters were not in his exclusive possession. But if the presumption arises only when the letters are shown to have been delivered to the addressee by the post office, the presumption may be rebutted by showing that the postal receipt was in its possession. [ 609 G H ] (3) There is no rule of law that an officer of the post Office who takes away all the letters must first deliver them to the payee concerned. When the post man has handed over the letters to the person who received them, the latter cannot be said to have retained them in his possession. The presumption will be raised if the letter is in the possession and occupation of the addressee. [ 610 A C ] (4) The mere fact that a number of letters are found in an al mir aya does not make the presumption that the holders of the letters had the opportunity to know the contents of the letter before delivery. The mere circumstance that the cheques were in possession of some person who might have been in possession would not make any difference since the presumption operates only when there is a clear indication that the person in possession was in possession.

The High Court, in exercise of its powers under Article 227 of the Constitution, has a duty to correct all errors committed by subordinate courts. It is not necessary that there should be an application for stay of proceedings before it and if such an application is made, it must be accompanied by an affidavit sworn to by the person authorised to administer oath s. In this case, however, no such affidavit was filed. The High court had issued notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be punished for contempt of court. The appellant appeared in the High Court on November 28, 1963 and raised several objections. On December 20, 1963, the High court passed an order staying further proceedings pending disposal of the appeal. The respondent moved another application for vacating the stay. The said application was rejected by the High. Court. Thereafter, the matter was taken up by the Ny aya Panchayat and the Ny ay alaya heard the parties. The Ny aya Panchayats then passed an interim order directing the Ny ya Panch as to continue the proceedings till the disposal of their appeals. The order of stay was vacated by the court on December 25, 1963. The two appellants who were present in the court stated that they would appear at the hearing of the appeals on December 23, 1963 when the Ny aye Panchayat adjourned the matters to January 27, 1964. The other two appellants also appeared on that day but did not appear. The Judicial Officer thereupon informed the Ny ayal ah that the Ny art ment proceedings could not be adjourned to enable him to appear. He accordingly went to the Ny ayat on February 11, 1964 and asked them to appear on that date. The appellants'advocate absent ed himself from the court. On March 10, 1964, the Ny ayam Panchayat adjourned to October 11, 1963 for recording evidence. On October 12, 1963 the Ny ayas arrived at the Ny i ad at about 5 p. m. and recorded the statement of the appellant No. 1. The Presiding officer prepared his report and sent it to the court along with the record. The court then directed the Ny aka to proceed with the matter. The judgment debtor challenged the order of the Ny arya before the High, Court which dismissed the petition. The appeal was allowed by the Supreme Court holding that the order was not final and conclusive and that the court was bound to take into consideration the statements made by the witnesses. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The order dated December 25. 1963 shows that the process of the court had been completed and the records maintained by the panchayat were signed by the Panch as. The fact that the record was not authenticated or certified does not make any difference. [ 121 D ] (2) The record produced by the appellant shows that after the order dated October 21, 1963 was passed, the record of the panchayat was not signed by any one of the Panch s. The record shows that on September 10, 1963 a copy of the order had been delivered to the Panch. The Sarpanch of the Gram Panchayat was present at the time of the passing of the impugned order. The Panch as were not examined. The only Decision and Holding: Officer was not present during the hearing. The question whether the record showed that the Panch was not properly served or that the records were not accurate was not decided. [ 123 F G; 124 A B ] (3) The High Courts have held that the proceedings are not vitiated by the fact that a person authorised by law to administer the oath's is not competent to do so. [ 124 C E ] (4) The provisions of section 105 of the Act are mandatory and the mere fact that certain reports are not accepted by the presiding officer cannot be regarded as a nullity.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, I. P. C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge on a charge of murder. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that the confession of the appellant to Uj agar Singh was not admissible in evidence as it had been made after the murder of Sheo Sahai; (ii) that there was no reason for Uj agar singh to falsely implicate him in the case; (iii) that he had no motive to kill Sheo Sahai and therefore his conviction could not be sustained.

The petitioners, who were elected to the Municipal Committee of Raipur in the election held in December 1978, filed a writ petition challenging the validity of the elections. They challenged the validity and legality of the notification issued under Rule 4 (1) of the Rules on the ground that it was not published in the Gazette as required by section 3 (2) of Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the publication of the draft electoral roll did not suffer from any illegality or infirmity so as to call for interference by the Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Courts have rightly rejected the challenge to the validity Of the impugned notification.

The appellant was a director of the company. He was prosecuted under section 135 (1)( c) of the Companies Act, 1913 for having failed to file his return of income and expenditure account in respect of certain companies. The directors were convicted by the trial court but acquitted him on appeal. On appeal the High Court held that the prosecution had not been launched against the directors as required by section 134 (4). In appeal to this Court it was contended that the failure to send a copy of the balance sheet and profit and loss account was a breach of section 133 (3) of'the Indian Penal Code and therefore the prosecution should be quashed. HELD: (i) Section 134 (2) of 1898 is an independent provision which provides that the general body meeting shall be convened every month at such time and place as may be fixed by the general meeting. It is not necessary that the number of members of the board must be mentioned in the notice of the general meetings. [ 19 F ] (ii) The proviso to section 134 makes it clear that if the general assembly fails to call a general meeting within 30 days after its being laid before the general committee, the general Meeting would be deemed to have been called. But there is no provision in the Act which requires that the period of 10 days should be given from the date of the last general meeting to be included in the general election. [ 20 G H; 21 A B ] (iii) The words " shall be present " in section 134 are wide enough to include the requirement of the section regarding the dates of the meetings and the date when the general will be considered. The expression " shall " in the context means " shall not be construed to mean " shall ". [ 22 E ] (iv) The word " shall'used in section 132 (4) does not mean that the General Body has to be constituted only after the general Board takes over the affairs of the Company. If the general Body decides to take action under section 134, it cannot be said that the Directors have to be sent to the Registrar or the Registrar.

The appellant, a public officer in the State of Hyderabad and a number of other persons were tried for offences under sections 120 B, 420, 467, 471, 477 A read with section 34 Indian Penal Code. The trial judge convicted the appellant and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years and fine. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted the accused but reduced his sentence to three months'rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the provisions of section 5 Of the Act did not apply to the case as there was no evidence against the appellant; (2) that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant had consp ired to commit the offence punishable under section 5 (1)( d) of the Act; (3) that even if the conviction was upheld by the High court, the appellant could be convicted only under section 4 of the Prevention of Corruption Act and not under section 161 or 165 I. P. C., and (4) that since the time when the courts below had acquitted the appellant, he was entitled to the benefit of doubt and hence the conviction must be set aside. HELD: (i) Section 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act does not lay down any inf lex ible rule which can be applied to all cases except those mentioned therein. It is not possible to hold that the provision of section 6 of the Criminal Procedure Code is bad because it does not empower the Government to direct an acquittal. [ 463 D ] (ii) The expression " otherwise than in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Code " occurring in section 5 of Act No. 1 of 1954 has been held to mean that the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure should be followed before making a reference to the High Courts for their orders. If the legislature intended that the provisions should be made applicable to trials and appeals, it would have expressly provided that they shall be applicable to all proceedings instituted upon complaints. But the Legislature did not use the words " save as provided in sub section (1)" in section 4 (1). [ 464 E F ] (iii) The word " otherwise " in section 6 (1), means " so far as may be necessary for the purpose of enabling the Court to take cognizance of any offence ". The word used in section 3 (1): " shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence charged ". There are two distinct provisions in the Act namely, section 5 and section 6. Under section 5, the charge is framed by the Court after taking into consideration the statement of the accused and the result thereof. The question whether the provisions are mandatory or directory arises only if the statute provides for such a contingency. The word'shall'in section 2 (c) is wide enough to include the recording of reasons for the conclusion. The reason why section 5 is cou ched in negative form cannot be im puted to the word'according to the context '. The word is normally con jun ctive ly used in order to qualify the word in its ordinary sense.

The appellant was appointed as a Professor in the Central Health Service, and he was promoted to that post. He was later promoted as an Associate Professor of Radi other apy in the same college on November 20, 1971. In 1965, the appellant was promoted as a Head of Department in the senior scale of Rs. 200 / p. m. On January 1, 1966, he was re appointed as Head of the Department of Orth opaed ics at the Government Medical College, Delhi. The appellant's appointment as a profess or in the said department was approved by the Government of India under r. 8 (2A) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1963. The relevant rules were framed by the Central Government in exercise of its powers conferred by section 16 of the All India Services Act, 1951. Rule 8 (2) provided for the constitution of a Selection Committee consisting of three members from each State. The first respondent was appointed to the post of Professor of radi ology in the General Duty Medical School, New Delhi. By a notification dated January 10, 1967, the Central Govt. constituted a Selection Board consisting of the following persons: (i) Dr. A. K. Bose, Additional Director; (ii) Dr.( Mrs.) R. S. An gi, Additional Secretary; (iii) Dr (Mrs.) A. R. An us ay i, Additional Professor; (iv) Dr, A. B. An al, Additional Principal; (v) Dr A. N. Roy, Additional Chief Secretary, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of india; and (vi) Dr S. R, An us hak u, Additional Commissioner, Central Health Services, New Secretariat, New Del h. The Union Public Service Commission, however, did not make any recommendation regarding the appointment of the appellant as Professor of Medicine in the general department. The respondents filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid order. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appointment was made by the President of the Indian Administrative Service and not by way of promotion. Allow ing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1) The expression " in the course of his service " occurring in sub rule (2A), means " in relation to which the conditions of his services have been fixed by the rules made by him under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution ". [ 77 D ] (2)( i) The word " in " is normally dis jun ctive and has to be construed so as to give it a meaning which it bears in ordinary parlance. It does not mean that the person who is actually holding a teaching post shall necessarily hold the same. [ 77 E F ] (ii). The words " in addition " are wide enough to include the posts mentioned in the second part of cl. (b) of sub rule 3 of r. 7. [ 78 G H ] (iii)( a) The words used in the first part of sub clause (c) of cl.( 1) of article 371 must be given their natural meaning. Decision and Holding: (a) that the expression " In the absence of the Governor " in cl. 5 (2), read with cl. 4 (a)( i), clearly shows that the intention of the fram ers of the Part is to exclude the requirement of the public servant concerned being a teacher in the former's private school, and (b), the expression'in the latter part of the sub clause would refer only to teachers in the previous schools of the same type and not to teachers employed in the other schools.

The Company, which was a public limited company, had been carrying on business as manufacturers of various products and in the manufacture of paper. It entered into an agreement with the workmen for fixing minimum wages at Rs. 75 per month. In addition to this, it also carried out certain other manufacturing activities including that of pain ting, printing and dy eing. The Company's employees were paid bonus at the rate of Rs. 9 per month by way of basic wage. The workmen claimed that they should be paid Rs. 85 per month instead of Rs 2 per month as fixed by the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the Company was entitled to a higher wage than what it was getting under the Minimum Wages Act. On appeal by the Company, the High Court set aside the award holding that the Tribunal was not justified in allowing the claim of the workmen. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that there could be no comparison or basis between the two sets of workers. [ 59 E ] (2) The fact that the workmen were given a lower wage than the one paid to them would not make any difference if the minimum wage is the lowest wage. [ 60 C D ] (3) The payment of bonus being based on the minimum wages, even though the workmen might have worked for some time, it cannot be said that the bonus is only calculated on the basis of the total wages received by the workmen from the Company. [ 61 B ] (4) The mere fact that there are three elements of basic wages will not justify the conclusion that the minimum rates of wages fixed by reference to the existing wage packet must be taken into account. [ 62 G ] (5) There can be no doubt that the dispute relating to fixation of minimum wages has necessarily to be dealt with by the Industrial Tribunal in accordance with the Full Bench Form ula. [ 63 F H ] (6) The question whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the matter in respect of the same industry is concluded by the decision of this Court in the case of Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd. vs Their Workmen;, referred to.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. In his return filed under section 139 of the Income tax Act he claimed that in respect of the assessment years 1959 60 and 1960 61 (i) he had not taken any steps to file a return under section 148 but only furnished information regarding his undisclosed income. He also stated that he could not have had reasons to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of the assessee to furnish full particulars of his income, he could no longer be said to have been in default. The Commissioner rejected this claim. On appeal the Tribunal held that the notice under section 147 was valid as it did not specify any reason for coming to the conclusion that it was a fit case for the issue of a notice under Section 148. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Dismis sing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The report submitted by the Income Tax Officer is not a fit one for the issuance of a show cause notice under sections 148. [ 249 B ] 2. The fact that the appellant's statement was recorded under section 151 (2) does not make out a prima facie opinion that the income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for that year. [ 250 G H ] 3. The question whether the Income - tax Officer had any material before him which could form the basis for issuing a notice Under section 148 arises only if there are reasons to find that the Income chargeable to income chargeable under the provisions of the Act is not satisfied. If the facts mentioned in the report do not satisfy the requirements of clause (a) or (b) of section 147 then the Income lax Officer cannot issue a notice. [ 251 F ] 4. The expression " reason to believe " in section 148 means " reason for immediate action ". It is clear from the report that the assessee had no reasonable belief that by reasons of the concealment of the income, the Income taxable Officer must give reasons for passing an order under section 150. [ 252 C D ] 5. The words " reason " used in section 151 are " reason, justification or jurisdiction ". They mean " reason ", " reason why I think it is a fit cases for the issuing of a search warrant or summons under section 132 " and not mere reason to suspect that the person who made the search should have some prima facie reasons to suspect the income liable to be assessed. [ 253 E F ] 6. The word " reason'used in sub section (2)( a) and (b), is very wide and includes reason to come to the conclusions. But where the circumstances mentioned in section 147 (2), namely, the time when the search took place, the period of time during which the search was required to be carried out would be excluded from the computation of the period prescribed under section 149. [ 254 A ] 7. The phrase " reason (s) " in relation to the proceedings under section 145 (2). is not defined in the Act.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1943. It had a branch at Bombay and it carried on business of manufacturing cloth, cotton tex tiles, cloth and other goods. In 1949 the appellant company entered into an agreement with its head office at Bombay for the purpose of carrying on the business of printing and publishing paper. Under this agreement the appellant firm agreed to carry on business as well as to carry out the business in cloth and yarn. Clause (4) of the agreement provided that the partnership would be dissolved by the death or retirement of any partner either by the deceased or by his heirs or by the assignee or heirs under the provisions of section 25 (3). Under clause (2) of that agreement the partners were entitled to apply for registration of their respective shares in the name of the appellant's firm. On April 1, 1939, the appellant applied to the Income tax Officer for registration under section 26 A of the Act of 19 18 which was granted but was rejected on the ground that there was no succession. The appellant then filed appeals before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the income from the business could not be said to have been taxed under the Act Of 19 18 because the business carried on by the appellant was merely a trading concern and not a business within the meaning of section 26 (2). The Tribunal also found that the business was carried on at two places namely, at Calcutta and Madras and therefore the appellant must be deemed to have carried on the same business at all. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The business of the assessee being one of the branches of the family of the appellants, the business must be treated as having been done at the place where the business is carried on; (ii) the business has been carried on only at Calcutta, and the appellant cannot be said in law to carry the business at Calcutta; (iii) the fact that the appellant did not pay tax at all when the business commenced at Calcutta does not mean that the whole business was dealt with at Calcutta. The business carried at Calcutta can be said only at the Calcutta address and not at Calcutta or at Calcutta nor at Calcutta at all; (iv) the appellant could not claim relief under section 25 of the Indian Income tax Act because the entire business was trans acted at Calcutta only at that place; (v) the amount received by the respondent as a result of the sale of the business cannot be regarded as profits earned by him in respect of the transaction of sale of goods at Calcutta since the business itself was carried at Delhi and the money was paid at Calcutta in full satisfaction of the liability arising at Calcutta even though the business continued at Calcutta till the time of the transfer of the assets of the respondent company.

The appellant, a Hindu widow of the deceased, was the sole surviving heir of her husband. She had two sons and three daughters. The first son died in 1955 leaving behind his widow, daughter and son. After the death of her father she applied for partition of the property by me tes and bounds. The application was rejected on the ground that there was no joint family or coparcen ary between the appellant and his brother. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant's claim was not barred by limitation as he had not been impleaded as a party to the suit. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the question whether the appellant was entitled to demand partition of his share under section 6 of the Bombay Act did not arise at all because the appellant had not challenged the validity of the partition nor could he be permitted to raise such an objection later when the question was raised before the trial court. [ 256 E ] (2) In view of the decision of this Court in Am ba Lal vs Laxman Lal ji (supra), the appellant cannot be allowed to contend that the respondent No. 1 was not entitled to get his share in the property. [ 257 B C ] (3) The appellant is not entitled for the partition of properties which were admittedly belonging to him but were inherited by his wife and children from her husband who were living with him. The appellant has failed to establish that the respondents are not entitled either to claim partition or to recover possession of any part of the properties. [ 259 D F ] (4) The contention that the heirs should be deemed to have been divided equally does not hold water. It is true that the proviso to section 6 refers to a partition effected after the date of the coming into force of the Act. But the proviso makes it clear that if a partition has taken place during the life time of the testator or after his death, the same shall be deemed for all purposes to be a partition. [ 260 A B ] (5) Section 6 of The Hindu Succession Act provides that where a male Hindu dies int estate without making a test ament ary disposition of his own property therein, then the property left by him shall be dealt with in accordance with the provisions of Chapter IV of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. Under the Explanation to section 7 (1)( b) of the Hindu Succession, the interest of the heirs of a female int estate shall be determined in accordance therewith. [ 261 G H; 263 A ] (6) The expression " Hindu W oman " used in the explanation means a person who is not a member of the tar wad. Therefore, the word " Hindu " in relation to a female Hindu would include a Hindu female as well.

The appellant Corporation was a statutory body constituted under the Andhra Pradesh (Regulation of Hindu Succession) Act, 1951. It had its own Board of Directors and it was registered as a Society under the provisions of the Andhra Area (Management of Personnel) Act. 1951. Under section 7 of the said Act, the Central Government is empowered to make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. Section 11 provides that subject to any directions issued by the Central government in this behalf, the Corporation shall be competent to frame regulations not inconsistent with the Act or the Rules made thereunder for carrying into effect the provisions thereof. In exercise of the powers conferred by section 11 of the Act, which are similar to those of the earlier Act, Parliament enacted the [ Staff (Control & Appeal) Regulations ] 1960. By virtue of section 1 (2) of the Regulation, the employees of the Corporation were entitled to continue till they attained the age of 60 years. The respondent filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the regulation on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the regulations framed by the Corporation did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the Central Govt. under section 11 (2)( b) of The Employees'State Insurance Act, 1948 is wide enough to take within its fold all matters incidental or ancillary to the main function of the corporation including laying down the conditions of service of its employees. [ 233 C D ] 2. 1 The expression " other employees " occurring in section 11 does not mean only persons who are employed in connection with the affairs of the Union but also include employees of an undertaking whose employment has been terminated either by the employer or the State Government. [ 234 E F ] 2: 3. The word " employee " used in section 2 (e) of A. P. Act includes every person employed by a company whether such person is a member of the armed forces or not. The definition of " employee ", therefore, cannot be confined to workmen directly employed by the corporation. [ 235 B ] 3. 1 If the term " employee'is defined to include any person employed on wages, hours of work, holidays, leave, wages, bonus, gratuity, provident fund, pension, gratuity etc., then the same would come within the inclusive part of the definition. [ 236 G H ] 3: 2. The words " other employ ments " in section II of the General Clauses Act, 1897 must receive their ordinary meaning. They must be construed according to the context of the statute in which the expressions are used.

The appellant was a Chief Minister of Haryana State. He was the Chief Minister in the State Government and he was charged with contempt of court for having published a pam ph let which contained certain li bel s, spe e ches, etc. The Chief Justice of the High Court refused to accept the apology on the ground that it did not contain any imputation against him. The appellant filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution praying for quashing the order of the Chief Justice. The High Court dismissed the application holding that no offence had been made out against the Chief Jus tices of the State. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) There is no substance in the contention that the letter was not a part of the duty of a Judge to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. [ 247 B ] (2) The letter dated 20. 2. 1975 contains a clear reference to the speech of Shri Mohan Singh, Chief Minister who was said to be a member of the Bar Association and to some other persons. It does not refer to any speech or expression either as a matter of fact or even a matter relating to poli tics. The letter merely states that " I am not willing to work ". The Chief Minister's speech cannot be construed as a statement of a person. A speech may amount to contempt if it appears to be calculated to interfere with his administration of justice. [ 248 C D ] (3) The words used in Article 124 (4) are wide enough to include a case where there is a prima facie case of contempt of Court. The word'sc andal ise'has not been defined in the Act. The meaning of the word def amation is given in Black's Law Dictionary, 5th Edition. But the context must be looked at from the point of view of the person making the imputation. The test is whether the imputation is intended to prov oke, inc ite or tend to depr ave or corrupt to the injury of any person or class of persons. If the imputation imput es a general tendency to sc andal ize the Court, the charge of contempt is not confined to such cases as are likely to result in embar r ass ment to the Judge but would also amount to sc utt le the administration of public justice. The Judges should be concerned in dealing with particular matters like the question of li bel or t abo tage of the judge. They should have a personal knowledge of the incident and they should know what the publication was about.

The petitioner was arrested on June 30, 1953, in connection with a case under section 5 (1) of the Indian Income tax Act. He was tried by the Special Judge, Delhi and convicted for offences under sections 120 B, 420, 467, 471 and 477 A I. P. C., and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years and fine. On appeal the Sessions Judge acquitted him but convicted him under section 409 I. PC. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the provisions of section 5 of the impugned Act were violative of article 20 sub clause (3) of article 19 inasmuch as they imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right of search without authority of law and were therefore void and un enforceable. Held: (i) The provisions of article 14 of the Constitution are not absolute in terms and there is no reason why the provisions contained in section 6 (4) should be read down so as to leave them out of operation after the coming into force of the said provision. (ii) Section 34 of the Penal Code does not off end against the equality clause enshrined in article 14 because it merely en acts a rule of evidence and gives an opportunity to the accused to prove his innocence. It is only when the court can say that the accused has been prejudiced or has been given a fair trial that the court may interfere with the order of acquittal. If the court comes to the conclusion that the prosecution has failed to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, the accused will have to be acquitted. But if the court holds that the trial has not been properly conducted the court cannot set aside the conviction.

The appellant Association was registered as a " commercial establishment " under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had its office at No. 271, R. K. Mittal's house, which is an integral part of the business of the Federation. In respect of the period from January 19, 1984 to February 28, 1983, it filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the said Memorandum and also for quashing the same on the ground that it violated articles 14 and 19 (1)( g) of the Constitution of India. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the activities carried on by the appellant were not " trade or business " within the meaning of section 2 (5) of Act, but they were only incidental or ancillary to the main activity of the fed eration. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression " commercial or industrial exhibition " used in section 2 of the Act must be given its ordinary meaning. [ 290 C ] 2. The definition of " commercial " does not take away from its purview any profit made by some process either directly or indirectly through out the activities of the association. The activity of a " public utility " may be a " trade " or " business ". But there can be no doubt that the activity carried on in the instant case by the club is a " business activity " within section 2 sub clause (d) of section 65 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. [ 291 B D ] 3. The activities carried out by the Appellant are " commercial establishments " within Section 2 (9) of The Indian Income Tax Act, 1961. [ 293 G H; 294 A ] 4. The appellant is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act and carrying on the business es of the various companies. Its activities do not fall within the definition of'commercial establishment '. Therefore, the activity of its members cannot be considered as'trade or profession '.

The appellant was the owner of an estate. He had a right to receive and recover rent from its predecessor in title, the respondent, under section 4 (3)( viii) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The income was assessable as income of the appellant for the assessment year 1949 50. In the accounting year relevant to the assessment years 1949 50 and 1950 51, the appellant received a sum of Rs. 36, 396 / as pension due on the mortgage of the estate. The amount was not taxable as income but only as pension. The appellant claimed that it was entitled to be taxed as such. Held, that the payment of pension by the appellant was not income within the meaning of section 2 (1)( b) of Income tax law. The pension was payable in perpet uity and not in perpet u ities. It was not a pension or pension. It is a pension which is given to an employee either by the employer or by the recipient. The character of the payment does not change merely because it is made after retirement. The payment may be voluntary or invol untary. It may be made before or after retirement or during his life. If the person who receives the pension dies, there is no reason why he should not be treated as receiving it when it is paid.

They were also entitled to be considered for promotion to the higher posts of Chargeman II under the Rules. In the year 1983 some of the Supervisors filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of the r equ ire ment dated 2nd February, 1981 issued by the Director General of Ordnance Factories, Ministry of Defence, Government of India, whereby it was directed that the appellants in the said writ petition would be entitled to all consequential benefits including arrears of pay and allowances. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that the respondents were not entitled to any relief. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allow ing the appeals, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The appellants are entitled to the same reliefs as were granted to the Supervisors'B's in the case of similarly situated persons who were given the same treatment as those of the petitioners in the instant cases. [ 11 C ] 2. 1 It is well settled that if an order passed by a competent authority is quashed or set aside by a court or tribunal, such order can be challenged in a writ proceeding. But where the order is held to be illegal or without jurisdiction, the principle of res judicata will not apply. [ 13 D ] 3 The principle underlying the doctrine of merger is that once the order of the Court is found to be erroneous, the subsequent proceedings taken in the matter of granting the relief must be held to have become infructuous. [ 14 G H; 15 A ] 3: 1 The principles governing issue of estoppel and res judicata are equally applicable to the present cases. The principle of constructive res judicata applies when there is conflict between the parties. [ 15 B ] 3 (i) The principle laid down in the above mentioned judgments is that the principle should be applied with regard to situations where the question of res judic ate is involved. [ 16 C ] (ii) Where the Court comes to the conclusion that the decision of the Tribunal is vitiated by fraud or misrepresentation, the court may direct the party aggrieved to approach the Court for appropriate relief. If he succeeds, then the Court may grant him such relief. [ 17 C ] 4. 1 In the instant case, the appellants of Civil Appeals Nos.

The appellant, a private operator of the State Transport Undertaking, filed applications before the Tribunal for grant of permits on various grounds. The Tribunal allowed the applications and directed that the appellants be granted permits in respect of the routes to which they were entitled under the scheme. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that (i) the proviso to section 63 (7) is not applicable to the case; (ii) that the application made by the appellant was barred by time as it did not comply with the requirements of the proviso; and (iii) that there was no justification for granting approval to the Central Government. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to Section 63 (1) does not contemplate any condition precedent to the exercise of power by the Central or the State Government under sub section (2) of section 68 D. [ 10 B C ] 2. The expression " other conditions " used in section 64 (7), means " such other conditions as may be prescribed ". It is clear from the language of the provision that the proviso is intended to apply only where the conditions are fulfilled. The word'conditions'has been used in the proviso so as to mean those conditions which are not covered by the proviso. The words " such services " have been used inter change ably in the Proviso to section 64 A (7). [ 11 E F ] 3. The object underlying the proviso was to enable the State transport undertaking to operate in different regions of the country. The main purpose of the Act was to give preference to operators of tourist vehicles. This was done keeping in view the interest of the general public and also to ensure that the sector operated by the State had its own prior ities. The intention of the legislature was to protect the interests of the travelling public. [ 11 G H ] 4. The provisions of the second proviso to s. 63 (6) are mandatory. They do not off end against article 14 of the Constitution. [ 12 E ] 5. The first proviso to sub section 63 is an enabling provision. It provides that the State may make rules providing for the grant of permit to private operators who are operating in the State of Karnataka. The second proviso is not confined to persons whose applications for permits are rejected but is limited to persons who have applied for permits after the date of the coming into force of the Amending Act. The third proviso to this section applies to all persons who are eligible for grant or renewal of permits under the Act. There is nothing in the said proviso which makes it obligatory upon the State to make any provision for giving preference to persons similarly situated. [ 13 E F;

The respondent was a registered dealer under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. On October 5, 1956 he sold his business to one M / s. S. A. R. Trading Company and another on October 5. 1956 for Rs. 12, 000. In the assessment year 1957 51 the appellant claimed that there was no liability created by the deed dated October 5,. 1956 as it was not an arrangement made between the transferor and the transferee but only a transfer of the business from the transferee to the respondent. The assessing authority held that the transaction was not liable to pay sales tax in respect of the turnover of the transferor. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government had power under section 19 (2)( c) of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee could be said to have been taxed with regard to the arrears of sales tax due by him up to the date of transfer. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression " any person or persons liable to payment of sales lax " occurring in section 10 of the Madras Act is wide enough to include within its ambit even those liabilities which are incurred after the sale of goods effected by the assessee. [ 66 C D ] 2. The word'assessment'used in section 19 of the Bengal Act must be read along with the words'assessment ','assessment '. Section 19 (1) of that Act defines the term'assessment ". The word assessment'has been defined in section 2 (b) of this Act to mean assessment made under the Act. The definition of assessment under section 2 of the, Act includes assessments made under section 23. [ 67 B E ] 3. The term assessment is used in the scheme of the Income tax Act. There is nothing in the Act which makes it obligatory upon the part of the assessee to file returns. If the assessee does not make the assessment, then the whole of the amount outstanding on the date when the assessment is made would become immediately due and payable. [ 68 G H; 69 A B ] 4. The object of the legislature in enacting the law was to provide for the recovery of arrears of tax due in respect thereof. The Legislature did not intend to lay down any such obligation. The intention of the Legislature was clear that the liability created under the statute should be one which was existing at the time when the tax was assessed.

The respondent, a Government servant in the State of Gujarat was dismissed from service by an order dated February 2, 1955. He filed a suit for arrears of salary and allowances under section 60 (1) of the Act claiming that he was entitled to be paid his salary during the period when he was suspended. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree on the ground that it was not proper to hold that the plaintiff had been asked to pay salary for the period between January 3, 1954 and March 5, 1955, as claimed by him. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the claim made by the appellant was barred by limitation under article 226 of the Constitution. [ 463 E ] (ii) The words " any other than breach of contract " in section 61 are wide words and include something more than tort s; but even so where a suit is brought by a Government Servant for arrears for salary, the decree may be passed if there is no such thing in the contract itself. But where a civil servant is entitled to receive the salary for a certain period or for some other reason, the payment of salary does not come within the purview of section 60 of the Bombay Re organisation Act, 1960. [ 464 B C ] (iii) Section 61 of the Bengal Ac commod ation (Requ isition ing) Act, 1947, which provides for the apportionment of assets among the two classes of persons mentioned therein, cannot be said to be either arbitrary or unreasonable. It is true that the word'person'in section 60 means a person who is liable to pay rent for the use or occupation of property belonging to another person. But the word " person " in its context must mean a person other than a person referred to in section 62 of the Rent Act. [ 465 G H; 466 A B ] (iv) The expression " person acting or purporting to act " in clause (e) of section 61 of Act includes a person acting in pursuance of a contract entered into before the appointed day with the consent of the landlord. The word " persons " in cl. (b) of sub section (1), therefore, refers to a person. The legislature has used the word, person in relation to a company. There is nothing in the Act which makes the company a " person ". The word'company'is defined in section 2 (h) of Act. The definition of " person ", however, shows that a company can be a legal entity only if it acts through or is connected with the company. The company is a jur istic person and the liability of the company arises out of the contract of employment.

The respondents were lessees of coal mines in the appellant's leasehold land. They had encroached upon a portion of the coal mine and removed coal therefrom. The appellants filed a suit for damages on the ground that they had encroached the entire area of the respondent's coal mines, but the trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to establish their claim. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High Court was right in holding that under section 3 of the Coal Mines Regulations, 1948, the Central Government has the power to exempt from operation of the Act any person who is an owner or lessee of a coal mine within its boundaries. Section 4 (1)( c) of the Regulation provides that no person shall be entitled to remove coal except in accordance with the provisions of the said regulations. The expression " owner " in this clause means the owner of the property and includes any person whose name may have been entered in the records of the company as the manager thereof. The word owner in section 2 (18) of, the Indian E ase ments Act, 1882 means a person who has acquired title to the coal mines. The definition of the term owner in the Regulation does not include a person other than the owner.

The appellant company was a private limited company and its employees were dismissed by the Government of Bihar under section 25 (1) of the. On June 21, 1958, the State Government referred an industrial dispute to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The reference made to it was numbered as Case No. 8 / 58. The award in that case was challenged on the ground that the management had not been given any opportunity to lead evidence before the tribunal and therefore the proceedings were vitiated. The Tribunal held that the employer could have led evidence before it but failed to do so. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The decision of the High Court is correct. [ 830 E ] (ii) It is well settled that if one is dealing with industrial adjudication, there is nothing more to be said and that prosecution should be quashed because it would result in prejudice to the management or public interest. [ 832 A B ] (iii) There is no provision in the Act which gives power to the appropriate Government to take action against an employee without giving him an opportunity of being heard. The only requirement is that he must be given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed dismissal. This requirement is satisfied in the present case. [ 831 D F ] (iv) The order of the Labour Appellate Tribunal dated December 6, 1952, shows that the appellant did not make any representation against the termination of service of his employees. The appellant's contention that the impugned order was mala fide and was passed after due application of mind and considering all relevant facts was rejected. [ 833 H; 834 C ] (v) The appellant has not been able to establish that the order terminating his services was mala fides or was passed by way of victi mis ation or unfair labour practice. [ 834 G ] (vi) The fact that the respondent had taken action under r. 18 (a) of Standing Orders in this case does not mean that the authority who made the order of dismissal was not aware of the real state of affairs.

The appellant, a tenant of a building in the town of Delhi was convicted by the Trial Court for an offence under section 115 read with section 77 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and sentenced to six months'rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court set aside the conviction on the ground that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the agreement dated November 27, 1954, was not a lease but only a licence. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order passed by the High court is correct and must be upheld. [ 442 E ] (ii) The question whether a party has been granted leave to file a suit or proceeding does not depend upon any decision of the Court. It is open to the parties to apply to the trial Judge for leave to amend their pleadings so as to bring them into conformity with the terms of the contract between the parties. [ 444 B C ] (iii) The power conferred by section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code is wide enough to include within its ambit even orders which are interlocutory in nature. [ 445 G H ] (iv) The expression " case " means all proceedings other than suits instituted in a civil court. The word " case ", in the context of section 115, includes a suit. [ 446 D ] (v) Section 115 of Civil P. C. confers powers on the District Court to call for records of a case pending before it from time to time. The power of the District Judge to call record of a particular case is restricted to the whole of the proceeding. [ 447 F ] (vi) The words " case decided " in section 115 have to be construed in the light of the facts of each case.
