The appellant was convicted under section 302 I. P. C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Sessions Judge, convicting him of an offence under section 304 Part II I. PC., and sentencing him to rigorous imprisonment for 10 years. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years'R. I. and directed that the sentences shall run concurrently. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) there was no evidence against the appellant in respect of his participation in the crime; (2) that the prosecution had failed to establish that he shared a common intention with others to commit the murder of the deceased; and (3) that even if the presence of the accused at the time of occurrence was doubtful, the case would fall within Exception 4 to s. 300 of the Indian Penal Code. HELD: (i) It is well settled that where the court entertain's reasonable doubt about the existence of a reasonable doubt, it has to determine whether the accused person has been prejudiced or not. [ 410 E F ] (ii) There are several considerations which should weigh with the court when considering the question of awarding death penalty. Firstly, the nature of the injury, the weapon used, the part played by the assailant, circumstances which may give rise to such doubts, the second the court's mind and the third ly, the opinion of the doctor as to the cause of death. Secondly, the condition of the last seen together with the opportunity for identification must be so serious as not to leave only a remote possibility of another view will not entitle the accused to claim the benefit of any doubt.

The appellant was appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court in exercise of his constitutional powers under Article 124 (4) of the Constitution. He was convicted for an offence punishable under section 5 (2) read with section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and fine of Rs. 1, 000 / and in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment of one year. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) Section 6 (1)( c) of Prevention of corruption Act is ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 (1) of Constitution inasmuch as it provides for removal of Judges at any time without the consent of the President; (ii) the power conferred by clause (e) of sub article (2), which enables the President to remove a Judge from his office, is not an un guided and un canal ised power; (iii) the order of removal passed against the appellant is invalid because he had been found guilty of misconduct within the meaning of clause (c) or (d) of section 5; (iv) since the appellant has been found to have committed corrupt practices, there is no question of his being removed from service within the purview of clause 2 (3) of Article 124 of the constitution; (v) the impugned order of dismissal dated 31. 7. 1980 is illegal and void; (vi) the appellant's appointment as Chief Justice of India is invalid and inoperative as the same is violative of the provisions of Article 217 (1); (vii) the respondent No. 2 having been appointed as the Chief Justice, he ceased to be a Judge and could not continue to function as such after the enactment of the Act; (viii) the High Courts and the Supreme court are not competent to examine the legality of the orders passed by them; (ix) the Governor of the State cannot issue any direction to the Chief Jus tices of all High Courts including the Chief Ministers of the States who were not members of Parliament at the time when the Act came into force; (x) the appointment of the Chief Minister is not valid in law; (xi) the appointments made by the Chief Secretary of the Government of Rajasthan are null and void and do not confer any legal right upon the appellant to continue as Chief Minister of the concerned State; (xii) the Chief minister of the Central Government is not entitled to appoint a Judge in his place; (xiii) the appointing authority does not have the power to appoint the Chief's of the High est Court or of the District Judge; (xiv) the executive functions of the Union are entrusted to the highest executive head of the judiciary and the said executive function is subject to the control of the Governor; (xv) the expression " other authorities " occurring in Article 12 includes the President and the Governor thereof; (xvi) the phrase " other persons " used in Article 311 (2)( b) means the President, or the Governor, as the case may be, Decision and Holding: (xvii) the word " person " in relation to the Executive Committee of the Council of States means a person who is duly elected to any legislative body and shall include a member of the Legislative Assembly of the territory of India; (xx i) " Public servant " means a public servant as defined in section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860); (xx ii) " Member of the Public Service Commission " means the Public Services Commission constituted under article 315 of the Con sti t ution of India. The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Caste in West Bengal. He belonged to the Bihar State which had been declared as a Scheduled Caste by the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950. On January 10, 1950, he made an application under section 16 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, praying that his election be set aside on the ground that he belonged to a Scheduled Tribe and not to a scheduled caste group within the Sun ri caste. The Tribunal held that the appellant's claim must fail because it did not establish that he belongs to a sub caste or a scheduled tribe group within any of the castes specified in item 40. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant is a member Of a Scheduled caste. [ 931 D ] (2) The evidence shows that the appe l l ant was born in the Bihar after the re organisation of States in 1956. There were no disputes between him and the appellant regarding the question whether he belonged, to the Scheduled Castes or to any other Scheduled Caste. It was also found that the evidence showed that the first respondent belonged to another caste called " Saha " but there was nothing to show that he was a Scheduled Castes. [ 932 B C ] (3) The fact that the tribunal came to the conclusion that the relevant date for determining whether the appellant belonged to any particular caste was irrelevant to the issue before it. [ 933 E ] (4) The finding of the Tribunal that the failure to establish that the person who bore the sur name Saha belonged to one of the two castes was wholly untenable. [ 934 G ] (5) The Tribunal rightly rejected the case of the appellant on the basis of the evidence adduced in the case.

The appellant, a tenant of the flat in dispute, was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate under section 18 (1)( b) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act, 1947. He filed an appeal to the Sessions Judge against his conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the appeal but reduced the fine to Rs. 30, 000. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) the term " relinquishment " used in section 18 means relinquishment of a tenancy as well as relinquishment of its tenancy; (ii) the word " relinquishment ", in the context, must be construed according to the context in which it is used and not in any narrow or technical sense; and (iii) the words " relinquishment of his tenancy " occurring in section 19 (2) mean relinquishment of the tenancy of the lessee. HELD: (1) The expression " relinquishment'does not occur in the Transfer of Property Act but in the General Clauses Act, 1897. It is a settled rule of construction that if there is no express provision to the contrary, the general meaning of the statute should be preferred to the ordinary rules of construction. [ 10 42 H ] (2). A lease may be determined by reference to the terms of the deed of transfer, but such a lease has to be for a definite period. If the intention of the parties was that the lease should be for an indefinite period, then the clause would have been worded differently. But where the language of the document is clear and unambiguous, the court cannot go behind the surrounding circumstances to find out what the intention was. When the legislature intended to convey a particular meaning, it could only refer to the intention expressed in the writing as a whole. [ 43 C D ] (3) The word " surrender " is not defined in the Act. The word'surrender'is generally used in the wid est sense to include a mere desire to retain possession after the period fixed therefor. The use of the word'relinquishment'in the English Dictionary shows that the word has been used in a restricted sense. [ 44 E F ] (4) The object of the Legislature in enacting section 18 is to prevent the breach es of the covenant by the tenant of his interest. The proviso to section 18 makes it clear that the landlord who receives any sum or consideration from the tenant shall be deemed to be a tenant. The words are " the lessor or one who holds his interest ". The words " the lessee or transferee " are wide enough to cover both the lessor and the lessee and they do not mean that the lessor has the right to receive the rent either directly or indirectly. [ 45 G H; 46 B ] (5) The words'assign s'are very wide and they indicate a choice between the lessee's interest and the property leased. They are not sy non y mous with the expression'assignment '. The latter part of the definition merely indicates that the former is meant for the benefit of the lessor.

The appellant company was a public limited company. It had entered into an agreement with the workmen for revision of wage scales and dearness allowance on the recommendations of the Wage Board, which was to be implemented by the Company. In the course of its business it introduced a scheme called " Dearness Allowance " in 1956 under which the employees were required to contribute at least 50 % of their total wages to the Company's account. On January 31, 1963, the Company passed a resolution that the pay structure of the Company should be raised from Rs. 150 / to Rs. 100 / per month. The Company also decided that the basic pay of the employees would be revised as per the existing pay scale. The company agreed to pay the minimum of the pay scale of Rs. 500 /- and Rs. 200 / respectively. The dispute relating to the fixation of the wage scales was referred to the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the Company was not entitled to any revision of the wages scales on the basis of the recommendation of the Pay Commission. The award of the Tribunal was challenged before this Court by way of a writ petition filed by the Union of India. This Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court. The matter was remanded to the Tribunal for fresh disposal. After remand, the Tribunal made an award directing the Company to pay to the workmen the difference between the minimum wage rate and the minimum wages fixed by the Award. The question arose whether the Tribunal could have directed payment of higher wages than what was paid to the other workmen who were parties to the settlement. The respondent workmen contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to go beyond the terms of reference and that the award was bad because it was based on irrelevant considerations. The contention was rejected by this Court. Dismis sing the appeals, HELD: 1. The Industrial Tribunal has power to revise or modify the wage rates. [ 227 C ] 2. The object of the Act is to provide better amenities to the employees. If there are two different classes of employees, one class will be preferred over another while the other may fall within the same category. The Tribunals are constituted under the Act to give relief to the employee. The Act does not contemplate a case where the industrial adjudic ator makes a departure from the normal rule of adjudication. But if the dispute is referred to an Industrial Tribunal, then the only remedy available to the aggrieved party is to approach the Labour Court under section 10 (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act. [ 228 A B ] 3. The expression " industrial dispute " occurring in section 2 (k) of Industrial Disputes (Central) Act, 1947 means any dispute or difference between an employer and his employees, capable of being referred to a tribunal under the. The word " industrial " is defined in section 3 (k), but the definition shows that it includes all disputes connected with or arising out of any provision of any of the items enumerated therein. Therefore, the dispute referred to for adjudication must relate to matters specified in item No. 1 of the Schedule. [ 229 D E; 230 F G ] 4.

The appellant company was awarded a contract for the supply of cotton to its customers. The respondent filed an application under section 15 (1) of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 before the Labour Court claiming that it had been paying wages to its employees and that the said award was binding on it. The tribunal held that the payment of wages by the employer would be governed by the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act and that there was no justification for the claim made by the respondent in respect of the period from April 1, 1940 to March 31, 1939. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the question whether the wages prescribed by the award were payable or not did not arise because the order of the Tribunal was not challenged by the employee.

The appellant was a public servant, and the prosecution against him was based on his act of receiving illegal gratification. He was convicted by the trial court under section 409, but the High Court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) sanction was not necessary as there was no valid sanction for prosecution under section 197 (1), and (2) that the sanction was invalid because the sanction did not state the reasons for doing so. Held, that the facts proved in the case showed that the appellant had received the money from the office of the Government and he could be prosecuted under section 5 (3) Of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, when he was a person who was acting or purporting to act as a public officer. It is well settled that the words used are not dis jun ctive ly; they do not con note a mere direction to an officer to obey or execute his orders. The word " may " in section 197, Criminal Procedure Code, means'must have been done in some manner in execution of their duty '. The expression " shall be deemed to be duly sanctioned " does not mean merely that the order must specify the particular official or officer against whom the offence is alleged to have been committed.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49. For the assessment years 1949 47 and 1950 51 the Income Tax Officer treated the profit or loss of the previous year as business profits and charged to tax in respect of that year on the basis that it arose in British India. In appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the word " income " occurring in section 2 (15) of the Indian Act did not include income from property which was taxable in British Indian State but was received or accrued in British Pakistan. On further appeal by Revenue the Tribunal held that section 32 (1)( ii) of 1922 Act applied to income arising in British East Afr ica and therefore the words " any person " in section 32 were wide enough to take within its fold income accruing or arising outside British India and so the proviso to sub section (1) of section 24 of the Act would apply to the case. Held, that the words'income, profits and gains of a company'in section 10 of the Income tax Act must be given their plain and natural meaning and they must be construed according to the ordinary rules of construction applicable to such cases. It is well settled that where the Legislature uses two expressions, one of which is qualified by the subject matter of the statute and the other defines it, the proper approach to adopt would be to enquire whether the legislature intended to give a restrictive meaning to the main provision and if the language of the clause is clear it would be permissible to refer to other clauses of the definition.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1946. It was a private limited company with its registered office at Bombay and it had been carrying on business of manufacturing, engineering and other allied industries. In the years 1948, 1950 and 1952, the appellant company entered into an agreement with its workmen for fixing the age of retirement at 60. On December 31, 1947, the Government of India issued a notification under section 2 (oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 requiring that all employees who had completed their service upto the age Of 55 should be retired by the Company from the date they attained the age specified in the notification. The appellant's case was that the age fixed by the Government was not binding on them as it was not based on any principle of law but merely on the basis of some decisions of this Court which were rendered subsequent to the decision of this court in Dun l op Rubber Co. Ltd. vs State of Madras; and it was contended that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the question of retirement age did not arise out of the award made by the Tribunal. Held: (i) The Tribunal has failed to notice that the principles laid down by this Court in Dun can & Co. vs Workmen, [ 1960 ] 1 S. C. R. 866, applied to the facts of the present case. (ii) The appellant workmen were entitled to the benefit of the decision in Dun n iram Limited vs Their Workmen,; (iii) The reference was bad because the Tribunal wrongly decided the matter without giving any reasons. The Tribunal had also mis directed itself in thinking that there was no clear evidence before it about the trend in the Bombay region to fix the retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60; (iv) the Tribunal has erred in saying that the trend was established in Bombay region when it said that the pattern of the Bombay Region was uniform throughout the country and that the practice of the Tribunal was erroneous and contrary to the provisions of the law.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1961. It had a large number of shares and its directors were also appointed as Directors. In 1959, the company was re organised with effect from May 19, 1965. On June 4, 1965, the Board of Directors of the Company passed a resolution that the business of the company should be trans acted by the company on behalf of M / s. L. A. Mit che ll Ltd., and that the appellant company would take over the management of the affairs of the said company. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated May 19. 1965. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the resolution of the Board dated April 2, 1965 did not off end section 23 (1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Division Bench held that the resolutions dated May 10, 1965 and July 9, 1965 were invalid and set aside the same. The appeal to this Court was allowed. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The resolution dated May 30, 1964 clearly stated that the company's business will be carried on in India and it was decided that the work of setting up of plant at the site of the factory will be done by the firm of L. As. Mit sub ishi p, the Managing Director shall be responsible for the implementation of the scheme. [ 347 C ] (ii) The fact that the Board resolved to constitute an agency under section 237 (b) does not mean that the decision taken by the Board is final. [ 348 B ] (iii) The word " committee " has been defined in section 2 (h) of, which means any person or body of persons appointed by the Central Government to perform the functions of such body. Section 3 defines the expression " committee ". The term includes any committee appointed by Central Government. Section 4 of the Act provides that the board may appoint one or more persons to carry out the functions assigned to it. Section 5 (1)( c) defines " committee ", according to which the Board shall consist of three members including the Chairman. The first respondent who was appointed as the Chairman of the Committee was removed from office by the President. The second respondent was appointed by him as Chairman of L, A.

The appellant was convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. He appealed to this Court by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) There is no evidence that the daco its had stolen property from any other source. It is not possible to say that they were in possession of the fruits of crime. [ 10 31 B ] (2) The offence was committed at night by as many as 20 persons who were the daco it themselves. In some cases there may be some more persons than others but none of them could have taken them away. Therefore, the presumption can be drawn in this case. [ 11 43 E ] (3) The conviction was correct in'all the circumstances of the case.

The petitioner was a registered medical practitioner. He was convicted by the Chief Medical Officer of the State for an offence under Section 5 (2) read with Rule 11 (1)( d) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1954 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500 / in default to undergo simple imprisonment for one month. On appeal, the Sessions Judge set aside the conviction but reduced the sentence from two years to five years'rigorous imprisonment. In revision, the High Court held that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case as it was not a case where the substance was found to be poison ous. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity of declaring the substance as poison for the entire country.

The assessee, a partnership firm carrying on business of money lending and other allied companies in the State of Bombay, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1952 53. In the course of its business, it received moneys from the Bombay firm as loans made in the ordinary course of the business of the assessee. It also received moneys by way of loan from the company. On receipt of the amounts, the assessee filed a return of his total income showing the amounts received by him as loans from the Company. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the amount had been transferred to the Bombay company and not to the company which had set up a capital fund. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sum received by the assessee from the Bank was not an allowable deduction under section 10 (2) (xi) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Tribunal further found that the monies sent by the appellant were not loans made out of any other business of its own but were loans made by the Bombay Company in the normal course of their business. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the Revenue. Dismis sing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the amounts paid by the Company to the Company are dedu cti ble or not is a question of fact and each case has to be decided on its own facts. [ 423 E ] 2. The principle underlying section 10 of the Income tax act is that where there is no dispute about the amount received by one party from another, the former must have regard to the circumstances of the case and the nature of the transaction and all the relevant factors including the financial position of the person concerned. If the assessee dis charges the burden of proof placed on him, he cannot be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 10. [ 424 C D ] 3. Section 10 (ii) of Income tax, 1961 provides that if any person fails to make a return under sub section (1), he shall, before furnishing such return, furnish a return thereof with the prescribed time and in the prescribed form duly signed and verified by him or by an affidavit sworn before a Magistrate or O ath Commissioner. [ 426 A B ] 4. The expression " any other person " in section 10 means persons who are liable to pay income tax under the Act. [ 427 G ] 5. The word'person'in section 2 (15) of The Indian Income Tax Act, 19 18 includes every person who is deemed to be a trustee under the Indian Trust Act, 1882. [ 428 F ] 6. The words " any person " occurring in section 11 (2)( vi) of that Act mean a person who carries on the business as a going concern. [ 429 H; 430 A ] 7. The term " person " used in section 13 (2), does not include a legal entity like a company. [ 431 D ] 8. The definition of " person ", given in section 65 (12) of Indian Income - tax Act applies only to a person being a resident of a particular country.

The petitioners, who were the owners of certain lands in question, filed Special Leave Petitions before this Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that they had not been served with a notice under Section 4 (1) of the Land Acquisition Act and that their possession was taken by the State Government without any valid acquisition. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that there was no material to show that the petitioners had approached this Court for such relief. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) the petitioners did not have an opportunity to meet the case of the respondents; (ii) the acquisition proceedings were vitiated because the petitioners'title to the land had already been acquired and the award had become final; (iii) the award was made within two years from the date of publication of the declaration under section 6 of the Act and therefore the period during which the writ petition was pending should be excluded; and (iv) the delay in making the award could not be condoned. Dismis sing the special leave petitions, HELD: (1)( a) The petitioners had come to court with un clean hands inasmuch as they had come with fr ank and full disclosure of facts. They had come up with fr ail's ి and had obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo to be maintained. [ 588 A B ] (b) It is well settled that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court with un convincing and un substantiated allegations would be liable to be dismissed. [ 589 C D ] (c) There is no reason why the petitioners should not come with a true and correct statement of fact. If they are able to establish that the award has been made within the stipulated time, then the petitioners can come with the same truth and cannot take advantage of the said fact.

The appellant bank was a banking company. It had been carrying on the business of providing loans to its employees in the State Bank of India, and it was doing so as an industry under cl. (ii) of s. 2 of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970. The appellant's case was that he entered service with the bank in January 1, 1959 when he was given the scale of pay of Rs. 100 but did not draw any salary as on January 1. 1959. He filed a suit for recovery of his salary from April 1, 1949 till November 15, 1964. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant bank had no right to fix his pay at Rs. 102. In appeal by certificate, the High Court held that the award of the labour court was correct and directed payment of one increment in accordance with the scale laid down in para. 5 of the Sas try Award. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The award of bonus is only an interim measure and does not affect the substance of the dispute between the parties; it is based upon the basic pay of the workman concerned which is fixed at Rs, 175. [ 1009 B ] (ii). The award is final and conclusive and cannot be reopened except in cases where the tribunal has made certain changes in the law after coming into force of the provisions of the amended section. The award passed by the labour Court is final subject to revision by the High court under section 115, C. P. C., and if there is any error apparent on the face of the record, the same may be corrected by the Labour Appellate Tribunal.

The appellants, who were the owners of a hotel, filed a writ petition in this Court under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of section 3 (1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 3 of the Act was not violative of Article 14 of the constitution and that there was no violation of any fundamental right. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (i) that section 2 (b) of an Act is unconstitutional as being violative of articles 14 and 19 (1)( f) of Constitution; (ii) that the provisions of the said Act are ultra vires because they take away or limit their inherent powers; (iii) that sections 3 (4), 5 (1), 6 (2) and 7 (2)( c) of Act No. 21 of 1952 which provide for the acquisition of property by the State Government and transfer thereof from one person to another within the same local authority, are violative of article 14 of Constitution inasmuch as these provisions violate the guarantee against arbitrariness guaranteed by article 14; (iv) that even if section 3 is held to be valid, the provisions are discriminatory and therefore void; (v) that Section 3 (3) of Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 is violative of the equality clause enshrined in article 14 inasmuch as the provision is discriminatory and unreasonable; (vi) that since section 3 provides for eviction of persons occupying premises without payment of compensation and also prescribes the procedure for eviction, section 3 has been violated; (vii) that s. 3 (b), (d) and (h) are violative Of article 14 and 16 of the Indian Constitution inasmuch the provisions have been made in contravention of the provisions contained in article 31 A (1); (viii) that sub section (3 C) of section 4 is violative Of the rights conferred by article 19 (l)( f). Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1). The expression " reasonable requirement " in section 3 does not mean mere absence of compulsion on the part of the owner of the building to carry out his obligations under the law. It is only when the law itself permits the exercise of such power that the question whether the condition imposed by the statute is reasonable or not arises. [ 281 F ] (2). The word'reasonable'in section 2 of the impugned Act means'adequate'or'not'unreasonable '. The words'sufficient cause'in the context do not necessarily imply that the requirement must be something which is known to the law and which is capable of being known by a reasonable man acting with ordinary care. If the circumstances justify the making of the order, the court may say so but it cannot satisfy the requirements of the section merely because the facts necessary to establish the existence of those facts are not stated in the notice served upon the petitioner.

The respondent assessee was a partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M / s. Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 having its registered office at Bombay. In the assessment year 1957 58 for the assessment years 1957 58 to 1959 60, the assessee claimed that it had paid income tax on the entire net wealth of Rs. 67, 560 /- by way of gift from the property held by it as partner in the books of account of the firm. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal holding that the gift was not binding upon the assessee because no profit accrued to the assessee in the hands of the done e or any other person. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the gifts were made by the done es to the wife of the assessee who was a partner in a firm with a bank and that the said gifts were effected by transfer out of the joint family funds which were shown in the accounts of the partners. The Tribunal also found that the assessee had not acted upon the gift by transferring an amount of Rs 1, 50, 000 to his son and this fact was brought to the notice of the Tribunal when the case was remanded. The High Court dismissed the reference against which the Revenue filed an appeal before this Court. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. 1 The gift is not a valid gift. It is a gift by transfer. [ 11 C ] 2. The gift of movable property is a valid transfer within the meaning of section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act. A gift of immovable property is not merely a transfer of immovable properties but is a conveyance of only a right to enjoy such property. If the donor transfers possession and control over the property he has a right not merely to enjoy it but to enjoy the same during the life time of the donor. Therefore, the gift is complete unless there is a transfer in respect thereof. [ 12 E F; G H ] 3. The object of the gift being to provide for the benefit of the transferee in the light of the provisions of the Act, the transaction is one of transfer of property. [ 13 B ] 4. The Gift Deed is a contract between two parties. The transaction is a sale of immovable estate. There is no statutory provision for the transfer of moveable property. The property is transferred to the purchaser for consideration. The price is payable either in full or in part. The value of the property is determined by the deed of transfer. The vendor may have a share in the property. But if the property sold is less than what is given then the property passes to the transferee. The title in the movable property does not pass to the transferor. The transfer is a condition precedent to the transfer. It does not create any interest in the immovable property. It only creates a right in the transferee to enjoy and enjoy the property without any let or hindrance. [ 14 D E ] 5. The word'transfer'means a transfer from one person to another. The expression'transfer ', therefore, must be construed strictly so Decision and Holding: (i) The words " transfer of land " do not mean absolute ownership. They are used in the sense of voluntary transfer. (ii) The transfer must be for valuable consideration. (iii) Such transfer must have been made in order to bring about the desired result. (iv) The expression " transfer " means a voluntary act of transfer and not a mere act of volition. (v) The word " transfer ", according to Con cise Oxford Dictionary, means something more than a mere desire. (vi) The term " transfer '' means a disposition of the whole thing or the whole of the thing conveyed, such as a transfer, delivery, payment, surrender, disposal, performance, worship or service.

The appellant was appointed as a District and Sessions Judge in the State of Orissa. He was posted as District & Sessions Judge, Ganjam at Berhampur on October 31, 1966. On November 1, 1965 he was transferred to the court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Ganjam, by an order dated October 5, 1965. The appellant challenged his transfer from the court at Berhampur to the district of Ganjam in C. S. No. 65 / 68. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the appellant had no right to continue in the post of District and sessions judge at Berhampur without the consent of the Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that the High Court erred in directing the transfer of the appellant from the District and Sub division courts to the administrative posts; (ii) that since the High Courts have not given any direction to the government to appoint officers in the secret ari at, the High court should be directed to issue orders of posting of officers in such posts; and (iii) that even if there is no such agreement, the power of the Governor would remain un affected. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts are not competent to issue directions or instructions to subordinate courts in matters relating to service conditions of judicial officers. [ 234 D ] (2) The executive cannot command the judiciary from being made responsible for every error committed by a court or tribunal while passing its orders. It is only when the executive acts with the best of its discretion and with due care and caution that the courts direct its action to be corrected. If the executive has acted within the bounds of law but does not act fairly, courts must intervene. [ 235 F G ] (3) The courts can interfere with the administrative decisions of the Executive unless they violate some rules or principles of natural justice. But where the executive fails to carry out the directions of the court, the courts will not interfere. [ 236 E ] (4) The power of control conferred on the High courts under article 235 is not intended to be exercised arbitrarily or capric iously. Where the High Cour thas taken over the jurisdiction of courts, their orders should be respe cted. [ 237 B ] (5) The scope of interference by the High. Court in the matter of disciplinary proceedings is very limited. [ 238 A ] (6) The powers of the High, Court under Article 226 of the Constitution are wide enough to enable them to correct errors of the kind which go to the root of the administrative or quasi judicial functioning. [ 239 H ] (7) The expression " superior courts " in article 229 (3)( b) of the constitution means all persons who are members of the civil services of the Union or of the States.

The appellant purchased the land in question from his co sharers. The respondent No. 1 filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the property on the ground that he was not the co sharer, but was only a co sharer. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to prove that the co sharers were entitled to pre emption under clause fourth ly of section 15 (1)( b) of the Act. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that the right of pre emption was conferred upon the co owners and not on the appellant's brother. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the appellant did not follow the procedure prescribed by the statute for getting the right over the land sold, the sale was void ab initio. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression'other'appearing in clause fourth is wide enough to include within its ambit even those who are co sharers who do not fall within the purview of clause fourth. [ 128 C ] 2. It is well settled that where there is no express provision to the contrary, the general principles of justice would be attracted. [ 129 D E ] 3. 1 Section 15 (2) of The Indian Evidence Act provides that when any fact is especially within the knowledge of one or more than one person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him. Where the evidence is clear, cogent and credit worthy, the fact must be such as would lead to an ir resis tible conclusion that the said principle has been violated. [ 130 G H; 131 A B ] 3: 1 The word " other " occurring in section 15 of the Indian Evidence. Code of Civil Procedure means " other things including things necessary to secure the ends of justice ". [ 132 F ] 2: 2. The word'other ', in the context of section 152 of the Evidence Act includes also the word'others '. Therefore, the word " Other'used in section 152 (1) of'the Act'in the inclusive part of section 151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure will have to be read e jus dem gener is with the words'other co sharers '. [ 133 B C ] 3.( i) The word I la qu es'in section 153 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 18 79 does not mean that the State Government can exercise the power of pre suming title of the land holder against whom the decree is passed. If the intention of the legislature was to exclude the State of Punjab from the scope of the expression'all other co owners'then the word I am referring to the State should have been used in the first three clauses of section 150 (1). [ 134 F H ] (ii) The expression " other co sharer " in section 155 (1), which is similar to the expression " co sharers ", in section 154 (1)) of the Maharashtra Land Reforms Act, 1960, means a coparcen er who holds land either jointly or separately.

The alien ees filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. They claimed that they were entitled to half share in the property as per the compromise decree dated 21. 8. 1987, which was registered on 21. 08. 1987. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the alienation made by Ses hi ah was not binding on the parties and the alien ees had no interest in the said property. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court and dismissed the suit. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the alien ee had no right created under the alleged sale deeds. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. 1 It is well settled that a transfer of immovable property creates an interest in immovable property unless there is some provision to the contrary in the Transfer of Property Act or any other law for the time being in force. [ 543 B ] 2. 1 Section 3 (b) of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 provides that where a person who has obtained a decree for specific performance of a contract against another for specific purpose fails to perform the obligation imposed by the contract, he shall be liable to account for mesne profits from the date of such decree till payment thereof. [ 544 G H; 545 A B ] 1. 2. The object underlying section 6 C is to prevent fraud and to provide for equitable relief to bona fide alien ees. The expression " without authority of law " in section 6 (c) of Madras Act XIV of 1939 means that the transaction should be acted upon. [ 545 D E ] 2.( i) The expression'lawful'used in section 2 (d) of Act 23 of 1983 is wide enough to include all transactions whether oral or documentary between a willing purchaser and a stranger transferee. The word'lawful ', as used in the context in which it appears indicates that the definition of'lawful title'is very wide. Its meaning must depend upon the context. The provisions of the Act are so clear that they will have to be construed strictly. [ 546 F G ] (ii) The Courts below have rightly held that the sale deeds executed by the purchasers in favour of the ven de es are valid and do not bind the alien ers. [ 547 B C ] (iii) The alien ee has no interest whatsoever in the properties, but only his legal representatives. He has no right to claim any benefit under the decree. [ 548 D ] (iv) The alienation made in favour is invalid and cannot be acted on. [ 549 E ] (v) The courts below have erred in law in holding that there was a compromise in terms of compromise deed signed by the parties. There is no agreement entered into by the ven ders with the ven er ent purchasers. The alien ations made by the alien ants are void able at their instance. [ 550 B ] (vi) The finding of the lower court that the compromise petition is genuine and lawful is based on evidence.

The appellants, who were the workmen of the two companies in Baroda and filed petitions under section 33 C (2) of the. Before the Tribunal, they contended that the sick leave granted to them was not a privilege leave as it had been provided for by the scheme of rehabilitation and the benefit of the sick company's sickness would be available only if there was an " industrial dispute " between the parties. The Tribunal rejected this contention on the ground that the appellants had failed to establish that the sickness benefit could not be granted to the workmen because of their inability to earn their livelihood because of the financial difficulties of the Company. On appeal, the High Court held that the Industrial Tribunal had committed an error in allowing the appeals of the workmen. In coming to the conclusion that the benefits admissible to the employees under the Act should be extended to the appellants, the Tribunal relied upon its decision in the case of A le mb ic Glass Industries Ltd., Baroda vs A le eve,; and observed: " It is true that the appellant has not produced any evidence before the Tribunal to show that the benefit which the workmen are entitled to receive from the respondent is not available to them. But the fact remains that the workmen have not been able to produce sufficient evidence to prove that the conditions of service applicable to them are not being fulfilled by the respondent. Therefore, the workmen cannot get the benefit under the provisions of the Act." The matter was remanded to the Tribunal with a direction to decide whether the workmen were entitled to the benefit or not. The appellants challenged the award of the Tribunal in writ proceedings before the High court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the reference since the question of sickness benefit did not arise out of the Award passed by the Tribunal. Hence the appeals by special leave. Allow ing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scope of the Reference under section 66 of the I. T. Act, 1947, is very limited. [ 10 39 F ] 2. The Tribunals constituted under the I & B. R. Act are quasi judicial bodies. They have to act judicially. They can only function within their own sp her es. They do not have the power to act as quasi judicial authorities. They are not courts but are quasi administrative tribunals. They must follow certain principles of natural justice. If they act arbitrarily or capric iously, they are subject to the rules of natural Justice. [ 11 D E ] 3. The awards made by the Industrial Tribunals are not open to challenge unless they are perverse or patently illegal. [ 12 G H ] 4. The Appellate Tribunal is not required to consider the merits of the case at the stage of admission itself. [ 13 B ] 5. The expression " industrial adjudication " in section 49 of the, is wide enough to include all disputes relating to the conditions or employment of persons employed in any industry. [ 14 E ] 6. The words " industrial disputes " occurring in section 46 (1)( b) of'the Act mean " industrial peace, national security and public safety ". [ 15 C ] 7.

The appellant was detained under section 3 (1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Sm ug g ling Activities Act, 1974. He made a representation to the State Government against his detention on the ground that he had been supplied with particulars which were not in accordance with law. The State Government rejected the said representation. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the grounds furnished to him were vague and there was no material before the detaining authority on which the subjective satisfaction could be based. HELD: (i) Article 22 (5) is an enabling provision and confers a discretionary power upon the detaining authorities to furnish particulars as well as the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest or not. [ 347 C ] (ii) It is true that the right to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22 (6) inasmuch as the obligation to communicate to the detenu the grounds on which such detention order is based has not been conferred in this case. But it cannot be assumed that the detaining Authority would have been able to disclose all relevant facts having bearing on the question of the reasonableness of the constitutional right guaranteed to the detenue under article 21. [ 348 A B ] (iii) The fact that the appellant's representation was received by the Government on the very next day after the receipt of the report of the Advisory Board shows that the Detaining Authority did not consider the same as sufficient and adequate particulars. [ 349 D ] (iv) There can be no doubt that the requirement of the Constitution must be strictly complied with if the grounds are not vague but only a few of them are so vague that they do not appear to be connected with the purpose of the detention.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army. He was tried by a general court mar tial for an offence under section 19 of the, which was held to be triable by a court mar ty e. The trial judge convicted him and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence from two years'rigorous imprisonment to that of fine. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, is ultra vires the. It was further argued that r. 15 of the said rules is ultra virus because it provides for the removal of a person from service when he is not subject to the provisions of the Act; (2) Rule 14 of Army Rules 1954 does not provide for the dismissal or removal of an officer without being tried and convicted by a criminal court mar ti als unless the officer has been tried by court mar l ace; (3) Rule 15 of Army Rule, 1954 does provide for removal of officers with whom there may be no court mar ily charged and who are subject to any of the provisions contained in s. 191 (2)( a); (4) Rule 16 of the Rules framed under the Army Act, 1954 requires that before a person is tried by the court mar ch the court shall record a finding whether the accused is guilty of the charge brought against him or not; and (5) Rule 17 of the Air Force Rules, 1953 provides that where a person subject to these rules is subject to a court - mar tial or is subject by the Central Government to the Act, the Central Govt. may dismiss or remove such officer. Held: (i) Rule 13 of the A ircraft Rules, 1950, is intra vires. (ii) Rule 14A of the All India Services (Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1955, is not ultra vires. [ 10 42 D ] (iii) Rule 18 of the Civil Service Rules, 1957, is also ultra vires as it is not repugnant to the provision of the Constitution. Rule 14 is not subordinate legislation. Rule 14A is ultra delegation of power to the Central government. Rule 15 is ultra section 44.

The appellant company was assessed to octroi duty in respect of certain goods. The assessment order was passed on January 14, 1964 and the tax was paid by it under protest. On February 25, 1963, a notice was issued to the Company asking them to show cause why octroi duty should not be levied on the goods brought into the octroi limits for consumption, use or sale therein. The appellant replied that the Company had no intention to levy octroi duty as they were collecting octroi from the public but did not pay it. The Panchayat thereupon served a notice upon the Company calling upon it to show causes why the octroi duty which was leviable should not he recovered from it. In reply the Company contended that the demand was time barred because ి had been received by it from the Collector of the District who had made it clear that the octroi was being collected from the Company's factory. The High Court held that the notice was valid and proper and dismissed the appeal. It also held that there was no justification for the levy of octroi duty at the time when the Company was found to be collecting octroi duty from the appellants. Allow ing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The resolution dated April 6, 1963 clearly stated that the resolution was passed after due consideration of the objections raised by the Company and the objections filed by the appellant. The resolution further stated that " the resolution will be taken up after the receipt of the report of the Committee ". [ 222 E ] (2) The words used in the resolution are " may " and not " shall " and therefore, the resolution is final. If the resolution does not say that the Resolution was passed without any qualification or limitation, it would be open to the Panchayat to impose octroi duty only if it could be done within the prescribed period. [ 223 C D ] (3) The word " may ", in the context means " may ". There is nothing in the language to warrant such a construction. [ 224 G H ] (4) The expression " may deem " in the first part of cl. (b) of r. 5 must mean an act done or purporting to be done in pursuance of a resolution passed by the Panchayat. The words " may think fit " in cl. 5 of the resolution do not mean that the action taken under the Act and the rules is required to be notified to the public. [ 225 A B ] (5) The contention that the words " shall be deemed " in r. 22 of the Rules cannot be accepted. The word'may'has been used in a wide sense so as to include all cases where the authority concerned considers it necessary to do so. The rule making power conferred by r. 21 is intended to regulate the exercise of the power vested in the Panchayat by r.. 22. The power can be exercised only by the President or Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti. The Rule requires that before a decision is taken by the panchayat, the Panchayat shall publish a notice of its intention to impose the octroi. The notice contemplated by r., 22 is a mere proposal to impose taxes.

The appellants were employed as workmen in the respondent company. They had been dismissed from service by an order of the Company Judge on a complaint made to him under section 31 (1) read with section 33 (2)( b) of the, and that they filed appeals against their dismissal before the Industrial Court. The Labour Court held that the conciliation proceedings were pending at the time when L ou is P ere ira was dismissed but it did not decide whether the conciliation proceeding should be continued or not. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The conciliation proceedings are deemed to have ended if no settlement is arrived at. If any settlement is reached, then the conciliation officer must start his investigation without delay and if for some reason the Conciliation Officer delays the submission of his report he may be guilty of a breach of duty. [ 10 42 D ] (ii) The object of the Act is to provide speedy and simple redressal to industrial disputes arising between employers and employees. It is true that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act do not contemplate the making of complaints after lapse of 14 days but only terminate the dispute which has already been referred to the appropriate Government. But there is nothing in the Act which prevents the conciliation officers from starting proceedings within a reasonable time. Section 12 contemplates that the Conciliation officer shall, within 14 days of the receipt of the notice under section 12 (6) of that Act, terminate the conciliation Proceedings. [ 1032 B C ] (iii) The scheme of the conciliation is that where a settlement is entered into during the pendency of the proceedings, the conciliation Officer will not make any award till such time as the conciliation work commences. The conciliation officer is required to submit his report within 14 weeks of the commencement of the strike. He is required under section 20 (2) to submit a report within 15 days. The period of 14 months would depend upon how soon the conciliation operations commence. The Conciliation Officer is required by section 12 to submit the report within the said 14 days. [ 1033 F H;

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the [ Prevention of Ill icit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988 ] (for short'the Act ') on the ground that he had been arrested without a warrant. He was arrested on November 3, 1985 and produced before the Magistrate on March 1, 1986. On the same day he was released on bail. In the grounds of detention it was stated that the detenu was in custody and there was no imminent possibility of his being released on remand. The detaining authority also relied upon the statements made by the detenu to the effect that he was in jail since June 14, 1985. The order of detention was challenged by him in writ petition No. 2 193 / 86 which was dismissed by the High Court on January 9, 1986 holding that the order of preventive detention was not valid as the detaining authority did not consider the material placed before him. The petitioner filed a Writ Petition in this Court challenging the validity of the order dated February 11, 1986 passed by the detaining authorities. This Court directed the State Government to dispose of the representation of the detenu within three months from the date of the receipt of the copy of the judgment. The State Government thereafter passed an order on December 6, 1986 rejecting the representation made by a detenu against his detention. The detenu preferred a representation against the said order but the same was rejected by the State Govt. The representation was rejected on April 8, 1987. Thereafter the petitioner moved this Court by way of a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the delay in disposing of the representations was fatal to the detention. Dismis sing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The delay in disposal of the mercy petition is not fatal to a person's right to make an effective representation. The fact that the representation was received after the decision of the Advisory Board would not be sufficient to invalidate the order. [ 10 42 D ] 2. The facts mentioned in the affidavit of the District Magistrate are relevant factors which have to be taken into consideration while passing the detention order. The grounds of habeas corpus were available to the detenu when the order was served on him. There was nothing to indicate that the detaining Authority applied its mind to the facts involved in the case. [ 43 G H;

The appellant was a dealer in bull ion and cas hew. He filed an application for registration of his firm under the Act on the ground that he had not been assessed to sales tax by the Sales Tax Officer, but the Assistant Collector of Central Excise issued a notice dated August 10, 1959 stating that the appellant's firm was a registered dealer and that the sale proceeds were being collected from him as sales tax. The appellant challenged the validity of sec. 27 (6) before the High Court which held that section 28 did not confer any arbitrary or un canal ised power upon the Administrator and that it conferred no such un canal ized and vague power on the Administrator. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. Section 28 confers wide powers on the administrator to grant or renew licenses for carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as dealer. [ 303 B ] 2. The object of the enactment is to prevent circum ven tion of the other provisions of the Act and by reference to which the Administrator is required to exercise his power. [ 304 A C ] 3. The expression " particular business " has been used in some of the clauses under section 28. It may be pointed out that the expression " special business " in sec. 28 means the business of buying and selling of goods and therefore the word'business'must be given its ordinary meaning. [ 305 F G ] 4. The words " general or specific business " are very wide and cannot be construed narrow ly so as to exclude from its purview trade or business carried on by a person who is not a trader or a retail er of articles of commerce or industry. [ 306 E ] 5. The word'region'in sec s. 28 and 29 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 should be read with the word " region " in cl. (g) of sec, 28.

The appellants, who were the desc end ants of one A in a temple and had been appointed as manager by another person, filed a suit for possession of certain properties alleging that they were not the true owners of the said properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the alien or was entitled to succeed to the properties only on the ground that he was the manager of the temple and that his appointment as manager was made under a mis apprehension of the law. The High Court held that the alienation was void because it was made by an incompetent man without any legal authority and that the property belonged to him. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Courts have taken the correct view of the matter. [ 133 B ] (2) It is well settled that if a Hindu alien ee takes up a position contrary to the wishes of the f ounder, such a transfer would be invalid unless there are circumstances which render it wholly un con sc ion able. If the alien ee has been removed from the management of the trust, the alien er must be deemed to have resigned his appointment. [ 134 C D ] (3) There is no force in the contention that the transfer of the properties in question was made with the object of defe ating the very purpose of the institution. [ 135 F G ] (4) The fact that the transferor and his family had been claiming beneficial interest in the properties all along shows that the transferee was acting as de facto man agers of the Trust. [ 136 E ] (5) The principle underlying section 120 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, is that where a trustee is a manager of a public trust, he acts as a trustee for the benefit of the public, but where the trustee has acted as a manager, he is merely discharging the trust. He cannot be considered to be a trustee in the eye of law. [ 137 H; 138 A ] (6) The provisions of section 119 of the T. P. Act do not apply to the present case since the transaction of the sale of the property in dispute was not one of'private trusts '. The High court was right in holding that there was nothing to show that the trustees of the appellant could be treated as persons exercising fiduciary capacity and therefore, the decree passed by the lower appellate court should be set aside.

The appellant, a partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M / s. Ved Gupta & Sons, filed a petition under section 3 (1) of the U. P. Cinema (Regulation) Act, 1952 for a declaration that the cinema theatre was not licensed to run by him or his authorised representative and that he had no locus standi to file the writ petition. The High Court dismissed the writ application holding that the licence granted to the appellant was not a licence within the meaning of section 2 (14) of'the Act '. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression " licensing authority " as used in section 3 of the Act is wide enough to include the authorities who are entrusted with the duty of granting licences under the Act. [ 594 G ] 2. The word " licensing " has been defined in section 2 sub clause (c) of section 3 to mean any person licensed under the provisions of the Cin emato graph Act, 1955. Section 4 provides that every licensee shall be deemed to be a licensee subject to the conditions contained therein. Sub section (3) of Section 4 of the said Act provides that no person other than a licensee or his agent shall be entitled to do any act which may be necessary for the proper conduct of the exhibition of cin emato graph films in a cinema. [ 595 A B ] 3. The definition of " licensing ", as given in section 4 (3)( b) of that Act includes the power to grant licences to establish cin em as and to hold meetings of the Board of Directors thereof. The words " licensing purposes " have been defined under section 2 of the Bombay Cin em as (Regulation), Act, 1949. The term " licensing purpose " is defined in the Act to mean the purpose of providing cin emato graphic exhibition of films. The Act defines the terms " licensing ". The definition also includes licensing of cin em ens. The definitions of these expressions show that there is nothing to indicate that the legislature intended to make such a distinction between licensing and licensing purposes. [ 596 C D; 597 F H; 598 A B ].

The appellants, who were the owners of a mill and had been allotted to them by the Custodian under the provisions of the, on December 2, 1954, filed a petition in the High Court for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to cancel the lease granted to them. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that it was not open to the petitioners to question the validity of the notice issued by the Administrator as he could not be said to have acted beyond his jurisdiction in issuing the notice under section 12 (1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The order of the High court is set aside and the matter remanded to the High, Court for its decision afresh. [ 213 A B ] (ii) The High Courts are directed to issue appropriate writs or directions to the authorities concerned in respect of the rights of the parties.

The appellant was a minor son of the deceased. He filed an application under section 225 (3) of the Act of 1955 for setting aside the order of the Sub Divisional Officer, Hanum angarh on the ground that he had not been given any power of revision by the Board to set aside the said order of Sub Divisional officer and that the appeal was dismissed by the High Court holding that there was no provision in the Act for review of its own orders. The appellant contended that the Board could not have reviewed its earlier decision without first reviewing it and that since the sub Divisional Officer committed an error in law, the High court should not interfere with his order. The High Court held that the question whether the Board had jurisdiction or not to set at n aught the appellate order of sub Divisional officer was not within the competence of the Board. In this appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (i) that the High Courts'powers were not available to the Board as they did not vest in them; (ii) that Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act of 18 56 did not empower the Board either to set up a new unit or to re assess the ceiling area; (iii) that even if the land holder had raised objection before the Board, the Board was bound to dispose of such objections after hearing all the parties concerned and (iv) that in view of the provisions of section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, the State Government was competent to set right the same. Dismis sing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Board is empowered to exercise its powers of superintendence over all revenue courts in order to regulate the functioning of'the subordinate courts so as to keep them within their respective sp her es of jurisdiction. [ 10 42 B ] 2. The expression " subject to the other provisions of the Constitution " in section 223 of the Government of India Act of 1935 means that the power of the High courts to set off any amount which may be found due from a person who has acquired proprietary rights therein would be vested in the Government. It is only where the High Commissioner is directed to dispose it of expeditiously, the power will lie with him.

The appellant, a newspaper establishment, published in the Gazette of India on June 20, 1981, published an article titled " Newspaper and Newspapers " containing the news items appearing at pages 1 to 8 of the paper book. The appellant was one of the publish ers of newspapers who had published the said article of publication. The first respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the award made by the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the publication of the said law reports was not a public publication within the meaning of section 2 (d) of the Act as it did not involve any publication of a newspaper. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The expression'newspaper'is defined in section 2 sub clause (b) of section 3 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 18 67 which defines'newspaper '. Section 2 (c) defines'daily newspaper'as under: " Daily newspaper means a periodical or periodical publication intended for the general public for the purpose of promoting the well being of the public." [ 565 C ] The definition of'newspaper ', as given in section 4 of the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 19 11, shows that the term'newspaper " has been used in relation to newspapers and newspapers. The definition contained in section 13 AA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 clearly indicates that the expression'daily newspapers'includes newspapers and the employees employed by the 1st respondent in their production or publication of such newspapers.

The appellant was a licensee under the Bombay Rent Control Act, 1947. He filed an application for leave to defend on the ground that he had not sub let any part of the premises and that he did not have any right to occupy the premises in question. The trial court dismissed his application holding that there was no evidence to show that he was a tenant or a sub tenant. On appeal by the respondent the High Court held that the agreement was one between the parties and it was a licence and not a lease. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in coming to the conclusion that the document was a lease and not as a licence. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression " sub letting " is clearly used in section 5 (4A) of the Bombay R ents, Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act. Section 2 (bb) defines a'sub tenant'as meaning a person who has acquired the right to remain in occupation after the determination of the tenancy. It does not include a trespasser. [ 890 E F ] 2. A sub tenant may be a sub lessee but if he is merely a licensee then sub tenant cannot be said to be a licensee within the meaning of the Act. But where the landlord himself occup ies the premises, the sub tenant becomes a deemed tenant under section 3 (a). Therefore, the word'sub'occurring in section 2 (6A)( b) will apply only when the sub lessee is a licensee and not the sub - tenant. [ 891 C D ] 3. The term'sub lease'means a subsisting lease from 1st September, 1965 till 31st March, 1966. If the sub lease is a sub lease, the same must be read as a lease because ి the sub tenancy would be a licence; but if the sub letting is made by a sub partnership, the licence is a licence, but if it is a lease, it is sub lease. [ 892 B C ] 4. The words " sub lease " are wide enough to cover a sub tenancy which can be terminated by efflux of time. [ 894 G H ] 5. The object of the provisions of the Rent Act is to prevent sub letting. The legislature has taken care to see that sub tenants do not suffer from the disability arising out of their relationship with the sub tenants. The Legislature has given a clear meaning to the expression'sub letting '. The expression'such sub tenant ', therefore, refers to a sub ten ement belonging to a particular class of tenants. There is nothing in the Act which prevents the legislature from giving a restricted meaning to a tenant who sub lets the premises. [ 893 C D, 895 A B ] 6. The word'Sub's idence'is defined in section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The definition of'tenant'in section 105 includes sub tenant also. The main purpose behind the Act is that a tenant should not be permitted to use the premises for more than five years. The Act makes a distinction between a tenant and a sub landlord. The concept of Decision and Holding: Under the Rent Control Acts, the status of a tenant is derived from the fact that the tenant is a tenant. The tenant is entitled to protection against eviction. The tenancy rights accrue to him under the Rent Restriction Act. The Rent Controller is empowered to grant leave to a partner in a firm carrying on business in the name and style of M / s. Bharat Electronics Ltd., and the sub partner is entitled for all the benefits conferred on a partner. The sub tenant is not a licensee. The licence is granted to a firm. The partners are entitled to carry on business at the premises as partners. The firm carries on business as a dealer and carries on its business as such. The partnership firm is a partnership firm.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1948 under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. Under section 3 of the said Act it was entitled to apply for a licence and pay a fee of Rs. 20 per annum on the total income of the Company as defined in that Act. The appellant claimed exemption from payment of Income tax by virtue of an agreement dated January 26, 1950 executed between the Maharaja of Jaipur and the United State of Rajasthan. The respondent contended that the appellant was not liable to pay any income tax or other taxes due under the law of the Rajasthan State but he was only liable to be taxed at the rates mentioned in the agreement. Held: (1) that the liability to pay income tax arose out of the covenant in the Co ven ant entered into by the Rul er with the Government of India and therefore the liability of the appellant did not arise by reason of the provisions of article 295 of the Constitution. (2) Article 295 (2), which is in Part B of the First Schedule to the Constitution, applies to the present case and the appellant could not claim refund of the tax paid by him because there was no recognition by the new sovereign.

The appellants were the owners of a large number of cotton textile mills in the State of Madras. They had been carrying on business as merch ants and importers, and also as importers. In 1949 they obtained licences under section 5 (1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, for sale of certain goods. On January 28, 1953, the Government of Madras issued a notification under section 4 of the Act exempt ing cotton tex tiles from the levy of sales tax. The validity of this notification was challenged by the appellants before the High Court of Madras, but their petitions were dismissed. The appellants then filed appeals to this Court. Held: (i) that the provisions of section 14 of the Bombay Act did not off end article 19 (6) of Constitution inasmuch as it provided only one exemption from payment of tax or purchase tax, which could be granted by the Government; (ii) that there was no provision in the Act requiring the owner of a factory to obtain licence for dealing in cotton tex tur ised yarn sold or offered for sale, and therefore, the provisions Of section 14A would not apply to such a case; (iii) that if the price paid for the goods purchased was not ascertain able, the said part of the price or the amount paid must be deducted from the price; and (iv) that even if the transaction was found to be one of sale of cotton, the entire turnover of the seller would be liable to be taxed at the rate prescribed by the Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. He appealed to this Court by special leave against his conviction, but that appeal was dismissed on the ground that there was no evidence to show that he had committed the murder. In the case of Bhil ia and Tuk ia, it was held that they were not guilty of murder because their acts did not amount to a pre arranged plan nor were they one done in furtherance of the common intention of all; that they formed an unlawful assembly with the common object of committing the murder of one person and causing grievous hurt to another. It was also held that the offence fell within the purview of section 326 of the I. P. C., and that the sentence of imprisonment for life imposed upon him was excessive. On appeal by special Leave, Held: (i) That the sentence awarded by the High Court must be reduced to transportation for life. [ 10 97 D ] (ii) There is nothing in the Evidence Act which shows that the two appellants were members of an unlawful association or were merely acting as such. If the two persons who participated in the attack are not concerned with the actual assault on each other, then the charge of abatement would fail. But if the two were not aware of the participation of each other in the commission of the crime, then, even though the act may have been done in prosecution of the same result, the accused cannot be convicted of the offence of murder.

The petitioner was a permanent Government servant in the Indian Administrative Service and he had entered into service on officiating basis. He was promoted to offic iate as Assistant Engineer with effect from 5. 11. 1976. On his retirement, he was reverted to his substantive post of Executive Engineer with retrospective effect from 6. 10. 1955. The order of compulsory retirement was passed by the Government under Fundamental Rule 56 (j) which provided that " if the Governor is satisfied after giving him a reasonable opportunity of being heard in the matter, that he should be compulsorily retired, then notwithstanding anything contained in Clause (i), he may retire at any time after attaining the age of 55 years but not thereafter." The petitioners who were in Class I or Class II service or post held between 25. 5. 1954 and 13. 8. 1974 were promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer with the respondent's lien. They challenged the orders of compulsory retire ment before the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal dismissed their petitions holding that they were premature since they had attained the age Of 50 years when they were compulsorily retired. In appeal to this Court it was contended: (1) that the impugned orders were violative of Article 311 (2) of the Constitution inasmuch as they did not give an opportunity to the petitioners to show cause against the proposed penalty of compulsory fi ance; (2). that the order of premature retirement was based upon the decision taken by the Union Public Service Commission in its meeting held on 3. 7. 76 and therefore, the impugned order was bad in law; and (3) that there was no warrant for the conclusion that the petitioners were in the class II service and post and hence they could not be compulsorily retire ed. Dismis sing the petition, ^ HELD: (i) The question whether the petitioners are in Class II or Class III service or posts can only arise if the power of compulsory retired has been exercised, the Government servant concerned cannot be said to have been in Class 1 or Class 2 service or the post on which he has entered service before attaining the prescribed age. [ 562 C ] (ii) It is well settled that where the exercise of power under Article 226 is discretionary, the court will not interfere with such discretion unless it is shown that the exercise thereof was made in violation of any mandatory provision of the statute or order. If the exercise is arbitrary or capricious, the fact that it is so, the High Court will decline to interfere. But if the action is mala fide or is made out of malice or extraneous considerations, the Court would not ordinarily interfere. [ 563 F G ] (iii) There is no rule of universal application that whenever a person is in the service or a post, whether substantively or in temporary capacity, he must be given a chance to satisfy the authorities about his claim. When a person holds a particular office or place, he is normally subject to the same penalties and restrictions regarding discipline as are imposed by the rules governing the conditions of his service.

The appellant Corporation obtained a proposal for insurance on behalf of the Life Insurance Corporation. The proposal was accepted by the Divisional Manager, who in turn forwarded it to the Divisional Office of the respondent No. 1. The Divisional Manager sent a letter dated 11th January, 1961 to the effect that the proposal had been accepted and credited to the account of the deceased with an endorsement " under protest ". The Divisional Officer wrote back to the appellant that the amount received by him should be credited to his account but he did not accept the same. The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of the balance amount together with interest thereon.
