The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no concluded contract between the parties and dismissed the suit. In appeal before the High Court, the appellant contended that the term'acceptance'occurring in section 2 (o) of the Act means'act of accepting '. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: The word'accept'is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as'act done or directed by action of a person in pursuance of some authority given in law to another." [ 565 E ] The expression'under written'has reference to the act of giving assent to one party over another. It is also clear from the dictionary meaning of the words'under writing'and'acceptance ', that the expression'at once'is used in the context of the present case. There is nothing in the said definition which would indicate that the word'under write'must be read as'under'or'at any rate '. The word " under stands'is normally dis jun ctive ly construed so as to convey the sense of the whole statute. But where the language is clear and unambiguous, the intention of the legislature is to be gathered from the context. If the words are clear and explicit, they must be given their ordinary meaning. Where the words of a statute are ambiguous, the courts cannot go behind the words in order to find out the real intention of Parliament. The question whether a particular provision is directory or merely directory would not therefore arise. [ 565 G H;

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the order of the High Court rev oking the certificate granted by the High court was not final and binding on them. The defendants contended that the certificate was not conclusive as regards the rights of parties in dispute, but only to the extent of the property which they claimed to be in possession of the plaintiff's father. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the certificates issued by the Deputy Commissioner under section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, were conclusive evidence of the title of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit. The High Court had held that the Certificate was conclusive and could not be acted upon. The question whether the certificate is conclusive or not did not arise because it was not necessary for the High. Court to decide the question of the nature of the controversy between the parties.

The appellant company was manufacturing cloth and the process or's expenses were being added to the assessable value of the processed fabric. The appellant claimed that it had paid excise duty on the processed fabrics manufactured by it, but the Assistant Collector rejected the claim holding that since the grey cloth had been sold in the market, the same should be included in the assessable price at which it was sold. The Appellate Collector held that the appellant was not entitled to any declaration as required under Rule 174 (2) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. In appeal before this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court erred in holding that the process of "'s expenses " would include the process ors'expenses, cost and charges plus profit. [ 173 E ] 2. The expression " goods owned by one person " used in sub section (1) of Section 3 of the Act means goods owned directly by another person. It is necessary to include the processing or manufacturing profit and the expenses plus the profit. Therefore, the High Court was right in holding otherwise.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 13, 1973. He was promoted to the post of Head Clerk in January 1974 and he continued to be so till April 1, 1975 when he was absorbed in Government service. On April 1. 1975, he was appointed temporarily as a peon by the Panchayat Samiti. In February 1974, he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his appointment as a Clerk. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the appellant had not been appointed as an ad hoc employee, he could not claim to be considered for promotion to the posts of a Head Clerk. Allow ing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The appointment of the appellant as a Head clerk prior to the date on which it purported to do so is valid and does not suffer from any infirmity. [ 751 D ] (ii) The appellant having been appointed on a regular basis, there was no question of his being entitled to be treated as a permanent employee or to be regularised as a servant. [ 752 F G ] (iii) The order of the High court dismissing the writ petitions did not call for interference.

The appellant, a Hindu Religious Institution, was the Mahant of a Math. He died in 19 17 leaving behind his widow and two minor sons as his heirs. On his death, the property devol ved on his son who died after the coming into force of the Madhya Pradesh Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948. The respondent filed a return claiming that the properties were acquired by him for religious purposes and not for personal benefit. The Assistant Commissioner held that the income from the properties was exempt under section 5 (1) of the Act and he assessed the income to tax at Rs. 40, 000 per year. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment but reduced the amount of tax to Rs. 45, 000. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Held: The High Courts have held that there is no presumption either way. There can be no presumption whether the property is the personal property or it is the property of the Math or the deity. It is only when the expenditure is incurred for the purpose of bringing the personal estate out of the income of the estate, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. The onus lies heavily on the person who claims exemption from the levy to show that the property belongs to the Math and the deity, and that the burden rests on the other party which fails to discharge the burden cast upon him. The burden of proving that the particular property is not the personal income of a Mahant is always on the individual and not on the one side alone. The mere fact that a number of properties are taken over by the Math cannot prove that the entire income is the income belonging to the institution. The income derived from the property must be deemed to belong to the math and the idol. The property of an idol is a personal property of its holder. The owner of the property may also have a personal interest in it. But where a nu cle us is installed in the temple, the ownership of the same will depend upon the income being earned therefrom. The source of income is not material. The ownership of a nu clear property vests in the idol itself. The nature of the user of the said nu cle ic property is immaterial.

The appellants were allotted lands in the State of Punjab. They had been allotted some other lands and they were also given possession of those lands by the Custodian, but their allotment was cancelled on the ground that there was no evacuee property. On appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 102 did not apply to a case where the allottee had surrendered his allotment or had taken possession of any other land. Held: (1) that r., 9 of the Administration of E vac uee Property Rules, 1955, which deals with cancellation of allotment is inconsistent with section 10 of the Act inasmuch as it provides for cancellation of allotments only on certain specified grounds and therefore r. 103 of the Rules does not help the appellants.

The recruitment of the two candidates was challenged by a group of successful candidates in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed that the results of the written examination be published within four months from the date of the judgment. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years'old examination could not have been lost and the public cause would not have suffered because of improper feeding into the comput e. Allow ing the appeal, this Court ^ HELD: 1. The recruitment process has been substantially com plied by completing the interview test and the result thereof has become final. [ 10 56 B ] 2. There is no justification for cancellation of the examination. The Public Service Commission had itself conducted the written and the fresh interview. It had also become final and could not be disturbed. [ 1057 F ] 3. The selection process has become infructuous as the fresh selections were made after the written test and interview. [ 1060 C D ] 4. The State Government is directed to re arrange the entire recruitment examine and make fresh selections. [ 1061 E ] 5. The appeals are accordingly dismissed.

The appellant, a member of the D era and its properties, was elected to be the ma h ant of the De ity. He filed a suit for possession against the defendants on the ground that they were the ma ths of the de facto ma h ants of the property belonging to them and that he had no right to manage the properties of the d ances in question. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the plaintiff's claim was not barred by limitation. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court should have granted leave to the appellant to prosecute the appeal as she had become the ma ha h ant only after the death of her husband. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court has rightly held that the appellant cannot be added as party under Order 22, rule 10 because she became the ma hy ant of her property. [ 491 G ] (2) The fact that she died during the pendency of the suit does not mean that she became a ma h ate owner of the estate. She becomes a ma hy ate holder of the ma hs than mo th of the properties appertaining to the subject matter of the case. [ 488 A B ] (3) The interest in the subject matters of the civil suit devol ved upon Shi am Dass who was elected as ma h anta of the m ou za of the District De ity in which she claimed to be she ba ad or the ma han of the village. [ 489 C E ] (4) The provisions of section 5 of the Act do not apply to the present case since the appellant was elected a ma hu a se as ma hs ar. [ 487 F ] (5) The proviso to section 3 (1)( b) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is not applicable to the facts of the instant case. It applies to the case of succession to the office of ma h ese ma h edar. [ 490 H; 490 A ] (6) Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not attracted in the instant cases.

The petitioners, who were working as Head Constables in the Indian Police Service (Group'C ') and posted at various places within the State of Andhra Pradesh, challenged the validity of the proviso to rule 2 introduced by the Government of India (Ministry of Home Affairs) Order No. 10 / 1 / 83 dated October 29, 1983 issued under the powers conferred by section 3 of the All India Services Act, 1951. The petitioners contended that they had been promoted to the posts of Head Constables on January 8, 1983 and thereafter on July 30, 1984, when the impugned amendments were made, they were not passed on the ground that they were arbitrary or unreasonable. They also contended that the amendment was violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it did not give any opportunity to the petitioners to show cause against the proposed action. It was further contended that there was no material before the Government for passing the impugned order and that the power to amend the Fundamental Rules was a legislative function which could be exercised only after the Legislature had considered the question whether the rules and regulations framed by the Governor would prevail over the provisions of the law. Dismis sing the Writ Petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The amending notification dated May 13, 1979 is invalid because it violates Article 309 of the constitution. [ 590 D ] (2) The amended rules are ultra vires the Constitution. [ 591 G ] (3) The amendment made to the Fundamental Rule 2 by the impugned Notification dated October 27, 1979 cannot be said to be bad in law since it does not suffer from any infirmity. [ 592 B ] (4) The retrospective amendment of the Fundamental rules is valid. [ 593 E ] (5) The impugned amendment has the effect of changing the conditions of service of the employees of the Central Government. The object of this amendment was to reduce the age of retirement of all Government servants so that those who have retired prior to the date of issue of the impugned notification can continue to serve till such time as may be decided by the appropriate authority. [ 594 F ] (6) The right to equality guaranteed by Article 14 of Constitution is not absolute but is subject to reasonable restrictions. [ 595 A ] (7) The fundamental rights guaranteed by clauses (a), (b) and (c) of article 19 (1)( f) are not absolute. They are subject to the limitations prescribed by article 14 and 19. These restrictions must satisfy the test of reasonableness and must be imposed by the legislature in the interest of public welfare. [ 596 H;

The appellants are dealers in various commodities. They were assessed to sales tax under the provisions of the C. S. T. Act, 1948 and the goods manufactured by them were sold by a dealer who was not liable to pay any tax under section 9 (1) or Section 6 (3). The assessees filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the said provision on the ground that it is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the retrospective amendment made in the year 1990 has no retrospective effect so as to off end article 19 (1)( g) of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the amendments introduced by the impugned amendment have no retrospective operation. Dismis sing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. 1 The amended definition of " turnover " in section 2 (p) of'the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, which defines " sale " means " any transfer of property in goods for cash or deferred payment or other valuable consideration, including a transfer of title in such goods otherwise than in the form and manner of the specified against such goods, by way of sale, gift, exchange or in any other manner but does not include a mortgage, hypothecation, charge or pledge; Explanation II.- For the purposes of this sub clause, " sale ", " purchase ", " transfer " and " delivery " do not include transfers of title to goods after their manufacture or production; [ 366 A B ] 1. 2 In view of the above discussion, the purchases effected by the assessees from the manufacturers / dealers during the period of assessment years 1985 57 to 1974 11, would be liable to tax at the rate of Rs. 4, 000 per ton ne of raw materials purchased by them. [ 367 D E ] 1: 3. The assessees had been purchasing raw materials for use in the manufacture of goods for which they were liable to be taxed at the point of purchase or sale. It was only when these goods were supplied to the assessees that they were taxed at a lower rate. Therefore, the assessees were not charged with any sales tax. [ 368 G H ] 2. 1. The levy of sales tax on the raw material purchased by the assessee was not based on any taxable event but was a mere incident of the contract between the manufacturer and the assessee. The price paid by the assesses to the selling dealer was not an ex gratia payment. [ 369 F ] 2: 2. The fact that the assessees did not pay tax on their sales and purchase within the prescribed time limit could not make any difference since there was no question of imposing any liability on the assessees. [ 370 E ] 2.( i) The words " subject to the provisions contained in section 5 (1)" occurring in section 6 (1), must be given its natural meaning and cannot be read dis jun ctive ly. The word " subject " in the context must mean subject to what is defined in the Act.

The appellant, a registered dealer, was assessed to purchase tax under section 10 (b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The assessment order was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and on further appeal by the State, the High Court held that the sales were exempted from payment of tax under article 286 (1)( b) Of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the words " a person " in section 10 of the Act mean only an individual who is not a registered assessee but a firm or company which is liable to pay tax under the Act. HELD: (i) The word " a " used in section 8 (b), must be given its natural meaning so as to include within its ambit every person who has become a registered one after the date of sale. [ 11 B ] (ii) The words " any person " are wide enough to include a registered person who is a registered manufacturer. It is true that the goods have been sold to another person who does not hold a valid certificate of registration; but that cannot make the declaration because the goods are despatched outside the State of Bombay. If such a person can be said to have made a false declaration of his intention he would be liable to prosecution under section 7 of the. But if the goods were not despatched by him or by a registered dealers they could not be said that the sale was effected by them in the course of export. [ 12 G H; 13 A C ] (iii) The expression " a registered. dealer " in clause (b)( i) of section 10 means a person who sells the goods to another and who is also a registered, dealer. Therefore, when the goods had been despatched by a person to whom he sells the same goods, the sale is taxable under section 9 (b). [ 14 D E ] (iv) The term'a person'in section 2 (d) of Bombay Sales tax Act includes a registered importer. The definition of'dealer'in the Bombay General Clauses Act, 19 04, is very wide and covers all persons who carry on business in the State. The Legislature therefore intended to levy purchase tax on the purchases made by a non resident dealer. [ 15 D E ]. (v) The use of the word " person " is restricted to a person whose name appears in the books of accounts maintained by him. The use and purpose of the words'a registered'and'a dealer'indicates that the legislature intended to apply the provisions of the sections to the transactions between the seller and the purchaser.

The respondent husband was the wife of a second wife. He filed an application for maintenance under section 125 (3) (b) against her husband and his family members, claiming maintenance from him at the rate of Rs. 300 per month. The Magistrate held that the respondent was not entitled to maintenance but directed payment of Rs 100 per month by way of monthly allowance in lieu of maintenance. On appeal, the Sessions Judge set aside the order on the ground that the amount had been paid as monthly allowance to the respondent's husband and that it was not sufficient to maintain herself. In revision, the High Court confirmed the view taken by the trial court. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 127 (3)( b) is manifestly to recognise the substitution of maintenance allowance by mutual consent. [ 80 E ] 2. The object and purpose of section 125 is social justice oriented which should be achieved by allowing the divorced wife to retain custody of the company during the pendency of the proceedings before the Magistrate. It is true that the word " divorce " has a very wide connotation and includes within its ambit any other kind of marriage; but this does not mean that the provision should be construed strictly or liter ally so as to render the divorce e and wife imm une from liability to prosecution. [ 81 F G ] 3. The proviso to section 125 makes it clear that where a person has given ir revocable authority to his wife to have a separate residence, she shall not be liable to pay maintenance to her after such divorce. This is what is meant by the expression " without reasonable substitute ". [ 82 A B ] 4. The words " without prejudice " are used in the context in which they occur. They do not refer to the specific instance of divorce e. The intention of the legislature is clear that the divorce es cannot be treated differently from their own husband. [ 83 D E ] 5. The language of section 127 (4) is plain and unambiguous. There must be a rational relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance. [ 84 C D ] 6. 1. The first payment made by the husband to his mother was towards the maintenance of his daughter who was living with him since 1962. The second payment was towards maintenance during the subsistence of the earlier two suits. The third payment was for the maintenance period commencing from February 1972 till January 1978. The last payment was made only on July 11, 1977. The subsequent payment was on account of maintenance for both these periods. The payment of the third payment could not affect the validity of the first payment. [ 85 H 86 A B ]. 2. Under section 125, the wife is entitled to receive maintenance from the husband if he has no independent income except the maintenance allowance. If the husband pays the maintenance amount to his credit, he will not be entitled to claim maintenance allowance under section 127. [ 86 C D ]. 3. Section 125 provides for maintenance of a divorced wife irrespective of whether she has a legal right to maintenance or not.

The appellant was a successful bidder in respect of the tender for the year 1988. He filed an application before the Collector, Samastipur on 25th March, 1988 under section 11 (1) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915 for cancellation of his bid. The Collector rejected the application on the ground that there was no requirement in the rule of natural justice to give any notice before black listing the appellant. The appellant challenged the order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State Government that the order passed by the Collector was not sustainable in law as the same had been passed without giving any opportunity to the appellant to make representation against the order. Allow ing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed is bad in law because it has been passed in violation of the principles of natural Justice. [ 10 B C ] 2. The impugned order dated 25. 3. 88 is set aside. The matter is remitted back to the Collector with a direction to pass fresh orders after giving notice to the petitioner and making representations against the said order.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he required the premises bona fide for his own use and occupation. The Rent Controller held that the respondent was not entitled to seek fixation of fair rent under section 10 (2)( vii) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 as amended by the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Valuation and Assessment) Amendment Act, 1965. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the question whether the building is a'public building'or not would be decided only after the Rent Controller has determined it in accordance with the provisions of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. Section 4 of the Tamil nadu Rent Control Act does not provide for any determination of the fair rent of the property. It merely provides for certain basic amenities which are essential for the proper functioning of the landlord's business. [ 571 C D ] 2. The object of the Rent Control Legislation is to prevent unreasonable eviction of tenants from their properties. If the legislature had intended to exclude from the purview of the rent control legislation such as the Rent Restriction Act, the Legislature could have provided for a machinery for recovery of the amount. But if the legislature wanted to make a law for determining what the fair rents should be, then it would have expressly excluded the applicability of the general principles laid down in section 10 of the Indian Rent Act. [ 572 F G ] 3. The power conferred upon the Rent contro ller by section 10 is an incidental power to determine the fair value of the tenanted premises. The legislature did not intend to deprive the owner of the right to claim higher rent from him. The statute does not contemplate a situation where the landlord may choose to avail himself of the remedy available to him under the Rent Act but seeks to enforce his right to ask for a higher rent than the one which is deemed to be reasonable under section 11 (2). [ 573 E H;

The petitioner respondent was a permanent and temporary officer in the Central Government. He was promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on ad hoc basis by an order dated 28. 6. 1969, issued under section 115 (1) of the States Re organisation Act, 1956. In his representation he had stated that he was entitled to be considered for promotion to the higher grade with effect from the date of his first promotion as Assistant Engineer. The petitioner's case was that he should have been given a proper consideration before the final list was prepared. The Central Government did not consider it necessary to give any opportunity to the respondents to make their representations. The petition was dismissed by the High Court. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Central Govern ment has to give a full and fair equ ation of posts which is a matter within the prov ince of the Central Gover nment. [ 107 E ] (ii) It must also take into account the relevant considerations such as the nature of the duties and responsibilities attached to them. If there are no rules governing the issue of seniority, the Central Govern mn t may decide whether or not to grant the same. But if the Central Govt. considers it necessary, it can do so only after consulting the State Governments concerned. [ 108 D F ] (iii) The power of the Courts to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equ ation is inherent in the provisions of the statute itself. [ 109 C ] (iv) The principle underlying the provision contained in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that where a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous considerations, such a decision cannot be interfered with by courts. [ 110 G; 111 A B ] (v) There is nothing in the Act which prevents the Central or the State Government from giving a hearing to the affected persons. [ 112 H ] (vi) The impugned order of the Tribunal does not suffer from any infirmity since it is based upon the recommendations of the Advisory Committee.

The petitioners imported canal ised items under the Import & Export Policy 1978 79. They filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of the said licences on various grounds, inter alia, that they were invalid for being granted Additional Lic ences and that the import policy prevailing at the time of import was discriminatory inasmuch as it had been done so arbitrarily without any rational basis and without any r hy me or reason. It was also contended that the petitioners had not applied for a licence to enable them to import their goods under the Additional Lic enses issued to them. The Customs authorities rejected the petitioners'applications on the ground that the imports made by them were not valid for a period of 12 months from the date of import and that there was no justification for extending the same to the petitioners. In the appeals before this Court, the petitioners contended that (i) the Additional licences which were issued to the Petitioners were valid for six months and the said period should be extended; (ii) the benefit of exemption notification could not have been given to the appellants because the Additional Licence was issued only to the extent of 10 % of the net foreign exchange earnings; (iii) the additional licences issued to other importers were valid only for a limited period of twelve months and not beyond that period; (iv) the order of the Collector of Customs dated April 18, 1985 was illegal since it did not give an opportunity to the petitioner to make its submissions against the said order; (v) the petitioners were entitled to import the goods under O GL No. 88 / 78 dated March 31, 1978; (vi) the import of canal ised item was permissible only by dealers engaged in the trade of sto cking and selling Dr y F ru its; (vii) the orders passed by the Government granting Additional Lic ens ors to the import agents were illegal and arbitrary; (viii) the impugned orders were violative of Article 14 of the Constitution; (ix) the respondents had acted arbitrarily in refusing to grant the Additional licenses to the present petitioners; (x) the conditions imposed by the Additional Licen sees are unreasonable and arbitrary and therefore liable to be struck down; (xi) the State has failed to establish that the Additional licen's ers were guilty of discrimination vis a vis the petitioners; and (xii) the provisions of the Import and Export Policy 1988 91 were not applicable to the case of the petitioners as they were not registered with the Central Excise Department. Dismis sing the Writ Petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners have failed to make out a case for interference by this Court under Article 32 of the Con stitution. [ 168 D ] 2. The Additional Lic encing Authority is empowered to issue licences to the applicants for import of goods which are permitted to be imported under the relevant Import Policy 1978. The power conferred upon the licensing authority to grant Additional Lic ene ry Lic ences is subject to certain conditions. The conditions for grant of such licences are specified in the Import Policy 1982 G. 0. This condition is incorporated in para 167 of the Imports & Exports (Control) Order, 1955. Clause 3 of the aforesaid Order provides that the licensee shall be Decision and Holding: " 3. The Licensing Authority may refuse to grant an Additional Licence if he is satisfied that the applicant is not suitable for the purpose for which he has sought the licence. 4. The licensing authority will have to consider the application received by him within three months after the expiry of the initial licence. If the licensing officer is satisfied about the suitability of the applicant for the licence he will grant the licence accordingly. 5. The licence holder will be free to sell his goods in the open market. 6. The licensee will be entitled to sell the goods manufactured by him in the course of his business. 7. The license fee paid by the licensee will not be refunded. 8.

The appellants, manufacturers of " Ro lled Jute Y arn " manufactured by them were paying duty on the value of the goods at the factory gate. They filed price lists in respect of the said goods and claimed that they should be assessed to excise duty under section 4 (1)( a) of the Act. The Assistant Collector rejected their claim for inclusion of the assessable value on the ground that the goods were not sold as such but were delivered to the buyer's premises or to their customers. On appeal, the Assistant Collector held that since the goods had been supplied by the buyer to the appellant's customer, it was not necessary to include the cost of packing in the assessable values. In further appeals, the Collector of Central Excise, Bombay, upheld the order of the Assistant Collectors holding that the value should be included in the value for determining the " value " of the excisable goods. The Revenue appealed against the orders of the Collector before the Customs, Excise & Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal which dismissed the appeals. Allow ing the appeals, HELD: 1. 1 The expression " cost of any packing " occurring in section 4 of the 1944 Act is only the " cost " incurred by the manufacturer while he is buying " the " goods ". [ 10 42 B ] 2. 2 The word " cost ", in relation to the " delivery " of " packing " means the actual amount charged from the buyer for the goods purchased and includes charges paid by the seller for the packing. It does not mean that the " costs " are to be included when the " sale price " is inclusive of the cost " of packing. [ 10 43 E F ] 3. The words " cost or component " in section 4A (4)( d)( i) of The Act clearly exclude in these matters the cost or element of the " Cost of packing " incurred " in addition to the price of the packing being collected by the assessee from the buyers. [ 11 C D ] 4. 1 Section 4 (4) (d)( ii) of Act provides that where the packing is of dur able nature and is returnable to the manufacturer, then the cost thereof shall be included. The proviso to this section makes it clear that the cost to be added to the assessable price shall also include the element of cost of transport. [ 1032 G H; 1033 A ] 2: 1 The question whether the cost has to be excluded from the assessable valuation of the cigarettes would depend upon the facts of each case. If the packing material is returned to the seller after packing, the same will have to be treated as if it was so returned to him.

The appellant was charged for an offence under section 5 (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and on a charge that he had received Rs. 100 from PW 1, the Assistant Superintendent of Police, who had taken the money back to his office in the presence of two independent witnesses, namely, PWs 1 and 2, and PW 3, the Manager of the Government Press at the relevant time. The trial court convicted him under section 161 I. P. C. and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year and also to pay a fine of Rs. 200 / with default sentence. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to six months'R. I. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt as there was no independent corroboration of the evidence of PW 1 and PW 2 regarding the demand of bribe made by the appellant. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: The presumption arising under section 4 (1) of Prevention of corruption Act is not attracted because the explanation offered by the accused is plausible. [ 506 A ] Section 5 (1)( d) of The Prevention of Money La undering Act provides that if any person has received any gratification other than legal remuneration or any valuable thing from any person, he shall be presumed unless the contrary is proved, to have been facilitated by such person, unless the said gratification or thing is Provided that where a person who has received a gratification as a motive or reward for doing or for bearing to do anything which he is not directly or indirectly authorized by or under any law for the time being in force, commits the offence of criminal misconduct, the presumption may be rebutted by proof of the circumstances mentioned in the said provision. It is well settled that the burden of proving the guilt of the accused rests on the prosecution and not on the accused. [ 507 G H;

The petitioner was a tenant of the respondent company. He filed an application under section 630 (1) of the Companies Act, 1956 for recovery of possession of certain property from his erstwhile employees and also to other employees of the company. The trial court dismissed the application holding that since the petitioner had not been able to prove that he was in occupation of any such property, it could be presumed that he had vacated the premises after termination of his employment. The High Court held that the words'any such officer or employee ', as used in sub section (1), were interpreted by this Court in Amrit lal Ch um vs State of Bombay [ 1968 ] 2 S. C. R. 197, but did not mean that the expression'any other officer or employees'would include officers and employees of a company within the meaning of section 630 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Section 630 (l)( b) is independent and distinct from its substantive provision contained in section 630. It does not merely indicate the nature of the property of the employer which may be said to have been taken away by the provisions contained in sub clause (a) of section 629 of the Indian Companies Act. The word " or " occurring between these two clauses must be read together with the context in which they occur. If the legislature intended to use the words " any such land ", then the expression " any other land " in cl. (a), would have been used. But if the intention was to exclude the land from being acquired by the Government, then the words should be read as " any land or building ". [ 179 D E ] (ii) The words " or land " are normally construed to mean land belonging to the owner or occupier of the land or the company, and not to the present officers or employees who occupy the same at the time of their appointment. [ 179 F G ] (iii) The expression " or any other property " in section 6 (1)( a) refers only to the existing officers or servants of the Company and does not necessarily refer to the future officers or persons employed in the past. The expression'such officer'means all those officers and servants of a Company whose office is either immediately or through the terms of employment.

The appellant was the owner of a large number of properties in the city of Nagpur. He had been managing the said temple for several years and he was looking after the affairs thereof. In the year 1948, the appellant's father made an application to the Charity Commissioner under section 72 (1) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, for the registration of the trust. The Assistant Charity Commissioner held that the appellant was entitled to be registered as a public trust under the provisions of the Act. On appeal by the respondent, the Assistant Charity commissioner allowed the appeal holding that the deity was not a private or public trust within the meaning of section 2 (13) of Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The primary object of the ded ication is to preserve the property for the benefit of the worship pers and to maintain them from deterioration and to make it available for worship at certain times in the interest of the public.

The Punjab Agricultural Income tax Act, 1939, was passed by the State Legislature in June 1946. Section 3 of the Act provided that no person shall be liable to pay any income tax on the sale of agricultural produce derived from land which is not grown and sold within the State. By section 4 (1) of the said Act, a notification was issued under section 3 of that Act exempt ing all persons who were owners of agricultural lands from payment of tax on their purchase or rental or any other purpose as may be specified in the notification. The petitioners challenged the validity of this provision before the High Court of Madras. The High Court held that the provisions of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 18 79, were ultra vires because they off ended article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the impugned provisions of section 46 (2) of that act were void being contrary to the principles laid down by the Privy Council in Pandit Ban arsi Das Bhan ot vs The State of Madhya Pradesh;, that there could be no question of discrimination between the two classes of persons similarly situated. That it was open to the legislature to enact a law with respect to one class of persons for the same purpose but that would not amount to an unreasonable classification violating Article 14 of Constitution.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1946. It had a total number of 22 employees and it was registered under the, as a body corporate under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. In 1956, the appellant company entered into an agreement with its employees for the use of night watch man's work at the head office of the company. The terms of this agreement were that the hours of work should be fixed by the company at the bottom of each hour of work. The workmen were to be paid overtime wages at the rate of one hour per day. The company did not pay any extra wages to the workmen on account of their having worked for more than nine hours. On December 15, 1955, the company issued a notice terminating the services of the workmen. The Company raised a dispute about the weekly holidays which were given to them from January 1, 1957 to April 30, 1958. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled to three days'weekly off every week but they were not allowed to work for more or less than 8 hours per day and therefore the provisions of section 13 (2) (c) of the, were not attracted. The Union contended that the provisions Of section 13 were not applicable to the case because there was no provision in the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1947, empowering the Government to fix the hours at which the workmen could go up. Held, that the contention must be rejected. The expression " working hours " occurring in section 13 means all time work including intervals for rest and does not mean that the normal working hours are only those hours of service. The definition of the word " hours " in section 2 (e) of that Act is wide enough to include the hours during which the work is done. The words " hours of duty " do not mean actual work performed by the workman at the place of work and not the ordinary work of the employer. The term " hours ", according to Web ster, means " such work as may be assigned to him by the employer ". The expression'hours of business'in section 12 (b) of this Act has been defined in section 4 (3)( d) of which it is said that the expression'daily'means regular or casual. Section 13 (3) provides that the employer shall not be bound to give any notice or other information to any person who is not employed by him. The proviso to section 13 gives power to the Central Government to make rules providing for the manner in which the period of work of any employee shall be so regulated. Under section 13 the appropriate Government can fix the working hours of the employees at 10. 00 a. m. and the maximum hours of over 11 hours of working per day cannot exceed 48 hours.

The appellant tenant filed a suit for eviction of the respondent on the ground that he was in arrears of rent from October 1, 1976 to October 30, 1976 and therefore it is not possible to evict him. The trial court decreed the suit but the appellate court reversed the decree. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that since the provisions of Section 20 are applicable only to suits which were filed after 10 years of the coming into force of the Act, the bar of section 20 would not be attracted. Dismis sing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. 1 The language of Section 2 (2) of the said Act clearly indicates that the provision contained therein will not apply if the field is covered by any other law or under any contract entered into between the landlord and the tenant. [ 167 E ] 1. 2 It is clear from the language of sub section (2)( b) of Section 38 that where the tenancy is governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the provisions thereof shall not apply. But where the provisions are made applicable to all suits except one set out in Sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 2, the proviso to sub section 2 (1) of that section provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of this Act, no suit shall be instituted for the eviction of a tenant except on specified grounds. [ 168 A B ] 2. 1. The expression " suit for ejectment " used in Section 20 means a suit instituted against a tenant for his eviction on the grounds specified in the sub sections of Section 39. [ 169 C D ] 2.( i) The words " suit " and " suit as defined in Section 2 have been substituted by the word'suit '. The Legislature has also used the words " Suit for eviction ". The legislature has deliberately used the expression " Suit " in the context of Section 40. Therefore so far as the protection given to the tenants under the Rent Control Act is concerned they will not be covered by the said section. [ 170 G H; 171 A B ]. (ii) The expression'suit for recovery of possession of any premises on the date of the suit'occurring in Section 37 (1)( iii) of this enactment does not include a suit by a landlord for recovery possession of the premises on title based upon title. [ 172 F ] (iii) The definition of'suit'in Section 12 (1), CPC cannot be applied because the legislature had not chosen to use the expression'Suit'in the Explanation to Section 20.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent landlord. On December 18, 1949, he filed an application under section 3 of the Act for ejectment on the ground that his tenancy had been determined by the Controller in accordance with law and not by consent. The Rent Controller held that the appellant's claim to be a th ika tenant could not be sustained as he had not applied to the contro ller before February 28, 1949. He also rejected the plea of bona fide requirement of the premises for occupation by the appellant. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 227 of the Constitution challenging the order of the District Judge. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1949 were applicable to the facts of the case and that the proceedings before the Controller were without jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (1) that the proceeding before the contro ctor was without jurisdiction inasmuch as no notice under section 4 of the Calcutta Thi ka Tenancy Act had been served upon him; (2) that there was no provision in the Act requiring any prior notice to be given before passing the eviction order; and (3) that even if the statute did not provide for such a consequence, the right to evict the tenant would still continue to exist. Dismis sing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) Section 4 of Act No. 5 of 1953 is prospective only and does not affect the right of the landlord to eject the tenant. [ 184 D ] (ii) The proviso to section 4 (1)( b) of the Bengal Thi ka Ten ant Act, 1948, which provides that where the rights of the landlords are not affected by any of the provisions contained in section 4 or section 5, the Controller shall give to the tenant at least one month's notice in writing specifying the grounds on which the right is to be exercised. This provision has been made subject to the other provisions of Chapter III of the said Act. It is clear from the language of section 4 that the legislature intended to apply to pending proceedings. [ 185 C E ] (iii) The expression " notwithstanding anything contained in any agreement " in sub section (2), means nothing more than what is provided in section 3. The word " suit " in section 2 (d) must therefore mean a suit instituted after the enactment of the rent laws. If the court is satisfied that the person who seeks to evict is a th ikar tenant, the court will have to proceed on the basis that the landlord has to show that the tenant is a successor to the t li ers. But when the matter is taken up in appeal, the appellate authority may go into the question whether the tenant has acquired any interest in the property. If he finds that the land is not liable to be evicted, he can pass an order of eviction against the tenant, but if he comes to the conclusion that the Land lord has not applied for possession, he may pass an appropriate order.

The appellant was appointed as Bench Secretary Grade I in the Central Government. He was promoted to the post of Bench Secretaries Grade II on January 2, 1986 and he was placed at serial No. 1 in the seniority list. On his promotion to the higher post, he was given a lower pay scale of Rs. 200 15 50. In the year 1987, the State Government issued an order fixing the pay of the appellant at Rs. 150 per month with effect from October 1, 1988. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to have equal pay for equal work. The appeal by special leave was preferred against this decision. Allow ing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of equal pay cannot be denied to the appellant because it is based on considerations of justice, equity and good conscience. [ 305 B ] 2. The concept of equality has a rational nexus with the object of Article 14. It must be determined by some method which is just, fair and reasonable. It means that equals are treated equally. If there is any ine quality or arbitrariness in the application of law or doctrine of classification, such differential treatment shall not be arbitrary but should be based on some qualities or characteristics of persons group ed together, and not in others who are left out. [ 306 E F ] 3. The impugned memorandum dated July 4, 1976 shows that the posts of Bench Secretary were being upgraded to the level of Joint Secretary Grade II. The posts of Assistant Secretaries were merged into one post of Joint Secretaries. The post of Assistant Secretary was equated with the post equivalent to the Joint Secretary (Selection) in the same grade. The promotional post was meant for direct recruits. The appellants were selected among the other two posts. The selection committee recommended their case for placing them at par with the other posts. There was no basis for the conclusion that the post was superior to the posts indicated in the order. [ 307 G H; 308 A C ] 4. The fact that the Commission recommended only one post for the post in question does not mean that the recommendation of the Committee was accepted. The recommendations of the Pay Commission were accepted. [ 309 D ] 5. The nomenclature of the post mentioned in the Government's letter dated 7 / 4 / 1976 is not conclusive. The nature of duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts are also different. The equ ation of posts made under the Government Order dated 10 / 11 / 1983 is based upon economic consideration. [ 310 E ] 6. The classification made under Rule 3 (3)( ii) of the Rules is based solely on the performance of the job. The function of the Government is entirely independent of the statutory duty cast on the authorities. The functions performed by the members of the Commission are not comparable with those of the employees working in the Secretariat. They are paid equal pay. [ 311 E ] 7. The Tribunal committed error in considering the fixation of pay in the cadre of the office of the Chief Secretary.

The appellant company, a private limited company, was granted the right to collect octroi from its customers in the State of Uttar Pradesh. In exercise of this power, respondent 1 issued a notice dated March 15, 1977 under section 68 (d) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 calling upon it to pay the property tax due on the lands and buildings within the municipal limits of the city of Delhi. The appellant Company filed objections against the proposed levy contending that the land or building was not liable to be taxed as such because the land was being used for purposes other than those for which the land revenue had been collected. The High Court held that the impugned tax was not leviable as there was no provision in the Municipal Act requiring the owner to impose any tax on lands or buildings. The question whether the land cess could be levied by the municipality was left open. The appellants contended before this Court that the provisions of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi Act, 1973, were ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature inasmuch as they did not provide for any machinery for imposing the tax. Dismis sing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. Section 127 A of the Municipalities Act, provides that the liability to pay taxes shall cease if the property is taken over by the Government without payment of any compensation. [ 128 C ] 2. The expression " any tax " occurring in section 127 A (3) of Delhi Municipal Corporation act, 1957, means " any sum payable by the owner of any premises, whether described as a rent or otherwise, under the provisions relating to the levy of property tax ". It does not include any duty payable by a person on the premises. The word'tax'has been defined in section 2 (b) of this Act to mean the tax mentioned in item 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. This definition includes taxes on lands and building. [ 129 D E ] 3. The contention that the expression " tax on land or buildings " in section 133 of the Bihar Municipal Act, 1950, must be read with section 133 thereof, is also devoid of merit. The legislature has enacted a law providing for levying property tax on the land and buildings. There is nothing in the Act which prevents the legislature from imposing a tax on these lands and structures. [ 130 G H; 131 B ] 4. The fact that the Central Act was made applicable to the area in question only to the extent of the land held by the appellant would not make any difference since the land tax is imposed on lands, buildings and properties. The Parliament has enacted the Act of 1973. The object of the Act is to prevent the evasion of taxes. The power conferred by section 125 of the said Act is not intended to be exercised by a Municipal Committee. The Act of 1960 is an Act to provide for the imposition of property taxes on land and building and for matters connected therewith. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is a special Act. The procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of that Act is substantially the same as provided in section 134 of the Bombay District Boards Act, 1920.

The appellant, a private limited company, was granted a lease by the Government of Madras under r. 47 (1) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 for a period exceeding one year and nine months. Under this rule the lessee was to pay annually the dead rent at the rate of Rs. 3 per month. The appellant's lease was renewed from time to time but it continued up to July 1, 1945. On September 21, 1955, the appellant applied to the Government for renewal of its lease in respect of the entire area of land comprised in survey No. 34 / 2 of village Ne th aji. The application was rejected on the ground that the appellant had failed to comply with the conditions laid down in r. 4 (1). The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the second proviso. The High Court held that the first proviso did not apply to the lease because there was no provision in the third proviso which made it obligatory upon the Government to make an application before the expiry of the lease. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The second proviso is only intended to make the right created after July 1. 1945, for a term which may be extended beyond one year or two years if the Government is satisfied that it is in public interest to do so. [ 158 D ] (ii) It is true that the third condition mentioned in the second Proviso is also satisfied in the present case. But the question whether the third Proviso applies to leases granted prior to July I, 1945, can arise only if the third ingredient is satisfied. If the third clause is read as a whole it would be clear that the three conditions set out in the first part are satisfied. The third condition is that the lease must be determined under the third part of the third. This condition is incorporated in the lease itself. Therefore, the third and fourth conditions have been fulfilled.
